abstract.p: Few concepts are as central to evolution as is fitness, and yet the quantification of fitness is often ambiguous. In particular, high-throughput experiments to measure mutant fitness in microbes are increasingly common, but vary widely in their definitions of fitness, which makes their results difficult to compare. What are the consequences of these different fitness statistics, and is there a best way to quantify fitness in a given context? Here, we systematize the set of possible fitness statistics according to the following three choices: (1) the encoding of relative abundance (e.g., transforming by a log or logit function), (2) the time scale over which to measure the change in relative abundance, and (3) the choice of a reference subpopulation for calculating relative fitness in bulk competition experiments, such as those using DNA-barcoded mutants. We show that these different choices can lead to significantly different interpretations of mutant fitness in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Escherichia coli, affecting the magnitude of fitness effects, the apparent presence of epistasis, and even the fitness ranking across mutants. This can confound predictions for evolutionary dynamics and gene functions. Altogether, our results demonstrate the importance of consistent fitness definitions for reproducible results across experiments.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The concept of fitness is supposed to describe the fate of mutations as they arise in a population (Gillespie, 2004) and defines other core evolutionary concepts such as trade-offs (Stearns, 1989). At the same time, fitness is often a confusing term in evolutionary biology (de Jong, 1994; Ariew and Lewontin, 2004; Kokko, 2021). It is possible to classify fitness measures by their role in theory (Smith et al., 2024) and their scale of measurement (Chevin, 2011; Houle et al., 2011; Wagner, 2010), but these arguments offer little guidance on how to measure fitness in practice. Empirical fitness measurements have become widespread in the microbial sciences—to test evolutionary theory (Paquin and Adams, 1983; Wiser et al., 2013; Kryazhimskiy et al., 2014; Levy et al., 2015; Nguyen Ba et al., 2019; Couce et al., 2024), detect microbial interactions (Schreier et al., 2023; Pierce et al., 2021), annotate gene functions (Wetmore et al., 2015; Price et al., 2018), and understand the spread of antibiotic resistance genes (Andersson, 2006; San Millan and MacLean, 2017)—but the approaches to quantifying fitness in these studies vary widely.

The classic approach to measuring the fitness effects of mutations uses pairwise competition experiments, where the mutant competes with its ancestral wild-type in coculture (Elena et al., 1998; Zeyl and DeVisser, 2001; Gordo et al., 2012). This approach is ideal because it mimics the dynamics of spontaneous mutations, and thus is typically used in experimental evolution (Paquin and Adams, 1983; Kryazhimskiy et al., 2014; Dykhuizen, 1990; Lenski et al., 1991; Spiers et al., 2002). For example, the Long-Term Evolution Experiment (LTEE) has evolved Escherichia coli over tens of thousands of generations and measured the fitness of each evolved lineage in competition with the ancestor (Wiser et al., 2013; Lenski et al., 1991; Barrick et al., 2023). However, pairwise competition experiments require a way to distinguish mutants from the wild-type in cocultures (e.g., fluorescent labeling or selection markers), which is not always feasible to engineer. A second approach is thus to measure properties of genotypes in monocultures, like the growth rate, and estimate relative fitness between genotypes from these measurements. Monoculture growth curves are straightforward to measure, even for large numbers of mutants (Warringer et al., 2003; Chevereau et al., 2015; Campos et al., 2018), but empirical tests have shown that the monoculture growth rate is insufficient to predict the relative fitness between genotypes (Concepción-Acevedo et al., 2015; Durão et al., 2021; Ram et al., 2019). Summary statistics of whole growth curves, like the area under the curve (AUC), perform better (Sprouffske and Wagner, 2016; Worthan et al., 2023; Schmitz et al., 2024). However, this approach breaks down for strains that engage in cross-feeding or toxin production, and attempts to improve monoculture-based fitness estimates require additional experiments (Ram et al., 2019; Schmitz et al., 2024) and do not go beyond qualitative fitness rankings (Schmitz et al., 2024).

A third and more recent approach is to measure relative fitness in bulk competition experiments using high-throughput sequencing, often of DNA barcodes (Levy et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2023). For example, transposon-insertion mutagenesis generates libraries of gene knockouts that can be tracked as they grow in a single batch culture (van Opijnen and Camilli, 2013). Estimating the fitness of each mutant allows us to identify genes that are particularly important in the growth environment (Wetmore et al., 2015; Price et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2020), in the given genetic background (Nguyen Ba et al., 2019; Couce et al., 2024; Johnson et al., 2019; Ascensao et al., 2023), and in the context of an ecological community (Schreier et al., 2023; Pierce et al., 2021; Ascensao et al., 2023; Martinson et al., 2023). Bulk fitness estimation also plays a major role in identifying beneficial lineages in experimental evolution (Levy et al., 2015; Blundell and Levy, 2014) (not unlike the tracking of viral pathogens in public health; Davies et al., 2021; Sohail et al., 2022; Meijers et al., 2023) and especially testing their fitness in new environments (Venkataram et al., 2016; Li et al., 2019; Kinsler et al., 2020; Bakerlee et al., 2021; Schmidlin et al., 2024). Many of these studies make different choices about the design of experiments and the calculation of fitness, without explaining why a certain fitness measure was used or how to compare between data sets.

The inconsistent choices for quantifying microbial fitness make it difficult to compare fitness across experiments, especially because different groups tend to use different definitions. For example, the LTEE reports relative fitness per-generation (Wiser et al., 2013; Lenski et al., 1991), whereas other evolution experiments exclusively report relative fitness per-cycle of batch growth (Kryazhimskiy et al., 2014; McDonald et al., 2011). New techniques, like barcode sequencing, often spark their own fitness metrics (Wetmore et al., 2015; Nguyen et al., 2020; Li et al., 2016; Frey et al., 2021; Gabzi et al., 2022). A different choice of fitness metric might lead to a different ranking of mutants in a genetic screen (and the importance we assign to those genes) or change statistical properties of the distribution of mutant fitness effects, which is essential to predict the probability of mutant fixation (Good et al., 2012), the speed of adaptation (Desai and Fisher, 2007), and the effect size in statistical tests of gene function (Wetmore et al., 2015; Price et al., 2018). This raises three key questions: (1) How do these fitness statistics differ? (2) Can we say which choices are optimal, in the light of first principles or some practical considerations? (3) Does this tell us how we should design these experiments? Previous work has addressed aspects of these questions (Smith et al., 2024; Chevin, 2011; Houle et al., 2011; Wagner, 2010; Matuszewski et al., 2016) but the arguments are scattered across disciplines and based on generic models of population growth (Smith et al., 2024; Chevin, 2011; Wagner, 2010; Limdi and Baym, 2023), rather than incorporating the specific dynamics of microbes in laboratory experiments. Here, we address these questions from a unified framework, using realistic microbial population dynamics with empirical traits to systematically test different fitness metrics.

sec.title: Results
Predictive power of fitness depends on the encoding of relative abundance
sec.p: We distinguish between three related but distinct notions of fitness (Smith et al., 2024), all based on predicting dynamics of a population (Mills and Beatty, 1979; Takacs and Bourrat, 2022; Charlesworth, 1993; Charlesworth, 1994). The first type of fitness is absolute fitness, which is a property of a single genotype by itself and serves to predict the change in the genotype’s absolute abundance N(t)\begin{document}$N(t)$\end{document} over a future time window Δt\begin{document}$\Delta t$\end{document} (Appendix 1—figure 1A). This is important for questions about extinction and evolutionary rescue (Alexander et al., 2014). The second type of fitness is relative fitness, which is a property of two genotypes as it describes how the relative abundance x(t)\begin{document}$x(t)$\end{document} of one genotype changes compared to the other over a time Δt\begin{document}$\(\Delta t\)$\end{document} (Appendix 1—figure 1B). This is important to determine the fixation probability of new mutations (Good et al., 2012; Kimura, 1962; Patwa and Wahl, 2008). In general, these dynamics are stochastic (Kimura, 1962; Hansen, 2017; Doebeli et al., 2017), but throughout this paper we focus on their average behavior across replicate cultures (as sketched in Appendix 1—figure 1C).

A practical challenge of working with relative fitness is that it must be measured between all pairs of genotypes in coculture competitions. Therefore, it is common to infer relative fitness of two genotypes based on some individual properties of the genotypes (Drlica, 2003; Sprouffske et al., 2018; Pinheiro et al., 2021; Diaz-Colunga et al., 2023). We denote this third notion of fitness as the fitness potential. Like absolute fitness, fitness potential is a property of an individual genotype, but unlike the absolute fitness, it has no meaning by itself. In analogy with the potential energy of physical systems, fitness potential is intended only to be compared between two genotypes (e.g., by taking the difference or ratio) to estimate the relative fitness between those genotypes (Worthan et al., 2023; Schmitz et al., 2024). The collection of fitness potential values across a large set of genotypes forms a fitness landscape (de Visser and Krug, 2014; Bank, 2022). Note that the term ‘fitness potential’ has been used with a related but somewhat different meaning in the population genetics literature (Manrubia et al., 2021; Kondrashov and Kondrashov, 2001; Milkman, 1978).

We emphasize that fitness as defined here gives information about short-time dynamics but not necessarily the long-term outcome (compare Smith et al., 2024). For example, this excludes the ratio of growth rates (Chevin, 2011; Diaz-Colunga et al., 2023) or the resource concentration R∗\begin{document}$R^{*}$\end{document} in chemostat equilibrium (Grover, 1997) since these quantities cannot tell you how fast the absolute or relative abundance is changing. We also note that in all these definitions, the fitness of a genotype is specific to one environment, including all abiotic and biotic factors. How fitness in one environment is related to fitness in other environments is important (Nguyen Ba et al., 2019; Price et al., 2018; Ascensao et al., 2023; Martinson et al., 2023; Li et al., 2019; Kinsler et al., 2020; Diaz-Colunga et al., 2023; Morin et al., 2018; Morin et al., 2022) but beyond the scope of this article, as we focus on specific laboratory measurements of fitness rather than abstract concepts.

In this article, we will focus on relative fitness as this is the most common object of high-throughput laboratory experiments in microbes (Wetmore et al., 2015; Lenski et al., 1991; Nguyen et al., 2020; Frey et al., 2021; Gabzi et al., 2022) and also has the most straightforward connection to key evolutionary outcomes such as fixation (Good et al., 2012; Kimura, 1962; Patwa and Wahl, 2008). We define a genotype’s relative fitness as any number that is sufficient to predict the genotype’s relative abundance x(t)\begin{document}$x(t)$\end{document} over a short time period (Appendix 1—figure 1). The simplest approach is to take a linear expansion of x(t)\begin{document}$x(t)$\end{document} and use its slope at time t to predict the change over a time Δt\begin{document}$\Delta t$\end{document} (e.g., Figure 1A, top panel):(1)x(t+Δt)=x(t)+dxdt|tΔt.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle x(t + \Delta t) = x(t) + \left .\frac{dx}{dt}\right |_{t} \Delta t.$$\end{document}

sec.p: The slope(2)slinear=dxdt|t\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{\mathrm{linear}}= \left . \frac{dx}{dt}\right |_{t}$$\end{document}
qualifies as a fitness statistic but often will incorrectly estimate the actual change in relative abundance because x(t)\begin{document}$x(t)$\end{document} is nonlinear (Figure 1A, top panel).

Alternatively, we can encode the relative abundance x\begin{document}$\(x\)$\end{document} in a new variable m(x)\begin{document}$m(x)$\end{document} (any smooth, strictly increasing function) whose dynamics may be easier to linearly approximate (Figure 1B; compare Denniston and Crow, 1990):(3)m(x(t+Δt))=m(x(t))+smΔt,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle m(x(t+\Delta t)) = m(x(t)) + s^{m} \Delta t,$$\end{document}
where(4)sm=dmdt|t\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{m}= \left .\frac{dm}{dt}\right |_{t}$$\end{document}

is the relative fitness under the encoding m. In Appendix 1—section S1 we show examples of the encoded relative fitness for an explicit model of population dynamics, and in Appendix 1—section S2 we show how this concept generalizes to absolute fitness as well.

The ideal encoding transforms the relative abundance x(t)\begin{document}$x(t)$\end{document} into a linear trajectory that can be fully predicted from the slope sm\begin{document}$\(s^{m}\)$\end{document}. While the log-encoding m(x)=log⁡x\begin{document}$m(x) = \log x$\end{document} is common in many TnSeq studies (Pierce et al., 2021; Wetmore et al., 2015; Price et al., 2018; Martinson et al., 2023; Morin et al., 2018; Morin et al., 2022) (and is implicit in plots of relative abundance on a logarithmic scale; Blundell and Levy, 2014), the log-encoded fitness slog\begin{document}$\(s^{\log }\)$\end{document} tends to overestimate the change at high relative abundance (Figure 1A, middle panel). Instead, the best encoding in most cases is the logit function (Figure 1A, bottom panel):(5)logitx=log⁡(x1−x).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle {\text{logit}}\,x = \log \left (\frac{x}{1-x}\right).$$\end{document}

This is because the relative abundance x(t)\begin{document}$x(t)$\end{document} typically follows logistic dynamics (Appendix 1—section S1), at least as a first-order approximation (Appendix 1—section S3, Appendix 1—figure 2), and the logit function is linearly related to the inverse function of logistic x(t)\begin{document}$\(x(t)\)$\end{document}. The logit-encoded relative fitness of a mutant is equivalent to the standard definition of its selection coefficient in population genetics (Fisher, 1930). For this reason we focus on the logit-encoded relative fitness for the remainder of this work. Note that the logit encoding and logistic dynamics apply to relative abundance and are not to be confused with the logistic growth model used with microbial growth curves, where it describes the absolute abundance (Zwietering et al., 1990).

sec.title: Estimating relative fitness requires a choice of time scale
sec.p: Since the relative abundance of a genotype can only be measured at discrete times, we must estimate the instantaneous relative fitness of Equation 4 using a finite difference between consecutive time points (Appendix 1—figure 1C, Appendix 1—section S4):(6)sm≈m(x(t))−m(x(t−Δt))Δt.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{m} \approx \frac{m(x(t)) - m(x(t-\Delta t))}{\Delta t}.$$\end{document}

For the logit-encoding this becomes(7)slogit=1Δt[log⁡x(t)1−x(t)−log⁡x(t−Δt)1−x(t−Δt)].\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}= \frac{1}{\Delta t}\left [\log \frac{x(t)}{1-x(t)}-\log \frac{x(t-\Delta t)}{1-x(t-\Delta t)}\right ].$$\end{document}

In the case of a single mutant competing against a wild-type strain, we can rewrite Equation 7 in terms of the log fold-changes (LFCs) of the mutant and wild-type strains:(8)slogit=LFCmut−LFCwtΔt,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}= \frac{{\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{mut}}}- \mathrm{LFC}_{{\mathrm{wt}}}}{\Delta t},$$\end{document}

where the LFC of each strain is LFC=log⁡N(t)/N(t−Δt)\begin{document}${\mathrm{LFC}}= \log N(t)/N(t-\Delta t)$\end{document} and N is the biomass of the strain. The LFC is sometimes also referred to as a Malthusian parameter (Wagner, 2010; Lenski et al., 1991; Alexander et al., 2014).

Therefore, a key element of estimating relative fitness from discrete time data is the choice of time interval Δt\begin{document}$\Delta t$\end{document}. There are two common choices in empirical measurements of microbial fitness. The first is to use a time scale extrinsic to the population. In particular, microbial populations in laboratory experiments (Lenski et al., 1991; Cooper, 2018) but also in some natural environments (Thaiss et al., 2014; Martin-Platero et al., 2018; Muratore et al., 2022) grow in discrete growth cycles dictated by external pulses of nutrients (e.g., batch culture). In this case, it is convenient to quantify relative fitness per-cycle, by choosing time units in Equation 8 such that Δt=1\begin{document}$\Delta t = 1$\end{document}:(9)scyclelogit=LFCmut−LFCwt.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{{\text{logit}}}_{{\mathrm{cycle}}} = {\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{mut}}}- {\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{wt}}}.$$\end{document}

The second common choice for Δt\begin{document}$\Delta t$\end{document} is a time scale intrinsic to the population, typically its generation time. The relative fitness per-cycle may depend on the number of generations in the growth cycle, and it can be valuable to normalize for this dependence, especially when comparing across environments (Lenski et al., 1991). However, defining the number of generations for a population with multiple genotypes growing at different rates is ambiguous. In the case of a single mutant competing with a wild-type, it is common to consider only the number of generations experienced by the wild-type strain, which is estimated by its log fold-change LFCwt\begin{document}$\mathrm{LFC}_{\mathrm{wt}}$\end{document}. It is convenient to express the generations in base e to match the natural logarithm in the logit-encoding, but this could equivalently be done by converting all logarithms in Equation 8 to base 2. Thus, the relative fitness of a mutant per-generation is defined by choosing Δt=LFCwt\begin{document}$\Delta t = {\mathrm{LFC}}_{\mathrm{wt}}$\end{document} in Equation 8:(10)sgenlogit=LFCmutLFCwt−1.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle {s^{\text{logit}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}= \frac{{\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{mut}}}}{{\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{wt}}}}- 1.$$\end{document}

This quantity is equivalent to the fitness statistic W=1+sgenlogit\begin{document}$W= 1 + {s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document} used in the LTEE (Lenski et al., 1991) and other studies (DelaFuente et al., 2020; Peterson et al., 2024; Moger-Reischer et al., 2023; Baake et al., 2019; Pearl Mizrahi et al., 2023). Some authors assume a fixed number of generations per growth cycle (Kryazhimskiy et al., 2014; Couce et al., 2024), but since this may not be true, we use the term ‘per-generation’ strictly for fitness statistics where the wild-type generations are explicitly measured.

sec.title: Relative fitness per-cycle and per-generation can rank mutants differently when wild-type growth depends on mutant
sec.p: Although relative fitness of a mutant per growth-cycle (Equation 9) and per-generation (Equation 10) differ only by choice of time scale, they are not just equivalent quantities in different units. First, while fitness per-cycle is well-defined regardless of whether the population undergoes net growth or death (Figure 1C), fitness per-generation is not defined when the wild-type undergoes no change or net death (denominator of Equation 10 is not positive) (Kokko, 2021; Lenski, 2021). This can occur for microbes under high drug concentrations, as well as for microbial populations under harsh environmental conditions as found in sediments or wastewater (Koch et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2022).

However, even when the wild-type LFC is positive, the relative fitness per-cycle and per-generation are not necessarily proportional to each other across a set of mutants competed against the same wild-type. The reason is that while the growth cycle time scale is extrinsic to a population and therefore the same across all pairs of genotypes, the generation time scale depends on the growth of the wild-type, which may be affected by the specific mutant it is competing against. This discrepancy can be quantitative as well as qualitative, producing different rankings of mutants. For example, Figure 1D shows two mutant genotypes (red and blue) that have opposite rankings under these fitness statistics: the blue mutant has higher relative fitness per-cycle scyclelogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}}$\end{document}, but the red mutant has higher relative fitness per-generation sgenlogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document}. The disagreement in ranking requires positive covariation in the LFCs (red bow tie-shaped area in Figure 1D), such that the mutant with higher LFC also induces a higher LFC in the wild-type (see illustration in Appendix 1—figure 3 and exact conditions in Appendix 1—section S5).

sec.title: Basic features of microbial population dynamics are sufficient to cause rank discrepancy between fitness statistics
sec.p: Since the discrepancy between fitness per-cycle scyclelogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}}$\end{document} and per-generation sgenlogit\begin{document}$s^{\text{logit}}_{\mathrm{gen}}$\end{document} occurs when the wild-type LFC varies across pairwise competitions with different mutants, we need to determine what biological mechanisms cause this. One way to explore this is to use a minimal model of microbial population dynamics parameterized by empirical data on a set of mutants. While a minimal model does not capture all possible mechanisms, it provides a null expectation for how common these discrepancies should be in real populations.

We use a model that approximates microbial population dynamics as three growth phases—a lag phase, an exponential growth phase, and a stationary phase (Figure 2A)—where strains compete for a single limiting resource with no other interactions (Manhart et al., 2018; Manhart and Shakhnovich, 2018), since resource competition is likely to be the main interaction between a wild-type and a mutant with only small genetic differences (e.g., a point mutation or gene knockout). This model captures the minimal dynamics of microbial growth under laboratory conditions, and therefore serves as a baseline for possible outcomes. We parameterize the model using growth curves of single-gene knockout mutants in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Warringer et al., 2003; Giaever et al., 2002; Appendix 1—figures 4 and 5, Appendix 1—section S6). We simulate a pairwise competition for each knockout against the wild-type (Figure 2A) and calculate relative fitness per-cycle scyclelogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}}$\end{document} and per-generation sgenlogit\begin{document}$s^{\text{logit}}_{\mathrm{gen}}$\end{document} for each knockout (Methods). While the relative fitness per-cycle and per-generation in the model are highly correlated across mutants overall (Appendix 1—figure 6), the model predicts major differences in individual mutants when we rank them by fitness (Figure 2B). Indeed, when we plot all simulated mutant competitions on the LFC diagram, we find that there are many pairs of points that have positive covariation in the mutant and wild-type LFC and thus give rise to rank differences (compare Figures 1D and 2C). Since these rankings often serve to select important mutants from a functional genomics screen or an evolution experiment, discrepancies between fitness definitions may lead analyses down different paths.

sec.p: This model therefore shows that the basic features of microbial population dynamics and resource competition with realistic parameters are sufficient to cause substantial disagreement between fitness per-cycle and per-generation, underscoring the importance of this analysis choice. Furthermore, the model reveals a basic mechanism that causes this discrepancy: mutants must have lower biomass yield plus variation in one additional trait (lag time or growth rate), and a high mutant relative abundance (e.g., 50%) at the start of the competition (Appendix 1—figure 7). These conditions are necessary because they allow mutants both to have variation in fitness and to alter the wild-type LFC in pairwise competition. Even though the wild-type growth rate is unaffected by mutants, the wild-type LFC will change in the presence of mutants that have lower yield because the population on average consumes more resources per cell division (Appendix 1—section S7). By this mechanism, it is possible to concoct a set of growth traits where relative fitness per-generation and per-cycle deliver completely opposite rankings (Appendix 1—figure 8).

sec.title: Fitness statistics can disagree on epistasis and long-term fitness trends
sec.p: Since the relative fitness of single mutants differs depending on whether fitness is quantified per-cycle or per-generation, how does that choice impact the apparent epistatic interactions between multiple mutations and the long-term evolutionary trend in fitness? Using the same minimal model of population dynamics as in Figure 2A, we simulate a set of six mutants, each one having an increase or decrease in each of the three quantitative traits in the model (lag time, growth rate, and yield), and calculate the relative fitness per-cycle and per-generation for all pairs of those mutations (assuming the mutation effects on the traits themselves are additive; Methods). We quantify epistasis as the fitness difference (in 1:1 competition with the wild-type; Methods) between the double mutant and the sum of the single mutants (Figure 3A; Krug, 2018).

(E) Hypothetical scenario for trait evolution in an evolution experiment. An evolving population decreases lag time to zero (orange line), increases growth rate until saturation (blue line), and gradually decreases biomass yield (green line). This trend is similar to initial observations from the Long-Term Evolution Experiment (LTEE) (Vasi et al., 1994). sec.p: Figure 3B shows that almost all the double mutants differ in their apparent epistasis per-cycle versus per-generation. Epistasis per-cycle occurs when one of the mutations affects growth rate (Figure 3C), while epistasis per-generation occurs when one of the mutations affects lag time (Figure 3D). This is because the effect of a change in growth rate accrues per-generation (and hence is non-epistatic when measured over that time scale; Appendix 1—section S8), while the effect of a change in lag time accrues once per-cycle (and hence is non-epistatic in the per-cycle statistic). See Appendix 1—figures 9–14 for growth curves in all cases. As an example, the double mutant in Appendix 1—figure 12, row D has two lag time-reducing mutations that are perfectly additive in the per-cycle statistic. However, the lag time mutations also reduce the saturation time of the growth cycle such that the fitness of the double mutant is spread over a smaller number of wild-type generations LFCwt\begin{document}${\mathrm{LFC}}_{\mathrm{wt}}$\end{document}, creating synergistic magnitude epistasis in the per-generation statistic. Note that this depends on measuring fitness for a mutant at relatively high abundance in the pairwise competition with the wild-type; when the mutant is rare, the wild-type fold-change LFCwt\begin{document}${\mathrm{LFC}}_{\mathrm{wt}}$\end{document} is effectively constant across mutants and epistasis measured per-cycle is proportional to its value measured per-generation (Appendix 1—figure 15). Differences in apparent epistasis can also lead to differences in apparent long-term trends of fitness per-cycle and per-generation in an evolution experiment. For example, if growth traits of a population in the minimal model evolve according to Figure 3E, then fitness per-cycle will saturate at an early time while fitness per-generation will continue to increase (Figure 3F). This is because the long-term decrease in yield reduces the wild-type LFC in 1:1 competitions between an evolved mutant and the wild-type, which causes fitness per-generation to increase (Equation 10).

sec.title: Different fitness time scales agree on LTEE trend but not on mutant ranking
sec.p: As an empirical test for discrepancies between relative fitness per-generation and per-cycle, we test how the choice of fitness time scale affects conclusions from the LTEE (Appendix 1—section S9). We reanalyze competition data from the LTEE (Wiser et al., 2013) using the relative fitness per-generation sgenlogit\begin{document}$s^{\text{logit}}_{\mathrm{gen}}$\end{document} (equivalent to the original definition used in those studies, W=1+sgenlogit\begin{document}$W = 1 + {s^{\text{logit}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document}) and relative fitness per-cycle scyclelogit\begin{document}$s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}$\end{document}. Note these competitions are between the ancestral wild-type and each of the 12 evolved populations, rather than single mutants, across time points. We confirm that the long-term fitness trend in the LTEE is the same for sgenlogit\begin{document}${s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document} and scyclelogit\begin{document}$s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}$\end{document} (Appendix 1—figure 16). When we look more closely at the fitness ranking between lineages, we find that the two statistics disagree on the fitness ranking at almost every time point (Figure 4A) and on the fittest population overall (Figure 4B; see Appendix 1—figure 17A for rankings). This discrepancy arises from positive covariation across pairs of LFC values in the LTEE competition data set (Appendix 1—figure 17B).

sec.p: While we have focused on the logit encoding so far since logistic dynamics are usually the best null model of mutant frequency dynamics (Figure 1A), the log encoding is common in many TnSeq studies (Pierce et al., 2021; Wetmore et al., 2015; Price et al., 2018; Martinson et al., 2023; Morin et al., 2018; Morin et al., 2022). The LTEE competition data is a valuable opportunity to empirically test the consequences of this choice as well. Figure 4C shows that the relative fitness per-cycle under the log-encoding scyclelog\begin{document}$s^{{\text{log}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}$\end{document} differs from the logit-based fitness scyclelogit\begin{document}$s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}$\end{document} for evolved LTEE populations, leading to ranking discrepancies especially for the fittest populations (Appendix 1—figure 18A). The discrepancy in fitness between encodings has a different mechanism compared to the discrepancy from fitness time scale: it arises from variation in the initial relative abundance in mutant-to-wild-type competitions in the LTEE data set. Although these pairwise competitions are intended to start with equal abundances of the evolved population and of the wild-type (1:1), Appendix 1—figure 18B shows that there is a systematic trend toward lower initial frequencies of the evolved populations over time. This trend is a side effect of the inoculation method in LTEE competition experiments, where a fixed volume of the evolved population is transferred to the competition growth cycle but the cell density for the evolved population in pre-culture decreases (Vasi et al., 1994; Grant et al., 2021).

sec.title: Fitness in bulk competitions is distorted by higher-order effects depending on reference subpopulation
sec.p: So far we have focused on relative fitness in pairwise competition experiments, but this is often not practical for large numbers of mutants due to the required strain labeling (e.g., with fluorescent proteins or selection markers). One alternative is to measure a fitness potential (as defined at the beginning of the Results section), such as growth rate or area under the growth curve (AUC) (Concepción-Acevedo et al., 2015; Ram et al., 2019; Worthan et al., 2023; Schmitz et al., 2024), from monoculture experiments, under the assumption that true relative fitness is proportional to the difference in this quantity between genotypes. Using our minimal model of population dynamics parameterized by single-gene knockouts in yeast (Figure 2A), we find that common fitness potentials perform poorly overall (Appendix 1—figure 19; see Concepción-Acevedo et al., 2015; Ram et al., 2019; Worthan et al., 2023; Schmitz et al., 2024 for empirical tests), with some success for the AUC but strongly depending on the choice of time window (Appendix 1—figure 20, Appendix 1—section S10).

Another approach to measuring relative fitness for a large number of mutants is to use bulk competition experiments, where many mutant genotypes compete simultaneously in a single culture and each genotype is tracked through high-throughput sequencing (van Opijnen and Camilli, 2013; Blundell and Levy, 2014). This raises the question of how well relative fitness of a mutant in bulk competition corresponds to its relative fitness in a pairwise competition with the wild-type, since the growth in bulk might be influenced by the presence of other mutant genotypes, a phenomenon known as a higher-order interaction (Morin et al., 2022; Manhart and Shakhnovich, 2018; Friedman et al., 2017).

An important choice in bulk competition experiments is the relative abundance of the library of all mutant genotypes compared to the wild-type. The invasion of a spontaneous mutation into an existing population is best captured by pairwise competitions with low initial relative abundance of the mutant (case I, Figure 5A), and one way to recreate this scenario in a bulk competition is to use a low relative abundance of the mutant library overall (case II, Figure 5A; Venkataram et al., 2016; Li et al., 2019; Kinsler et al., 2020; Bakerlee et al., 2021; Schmidlin et al., 2024). A practical problem with case II is that individual genotypes in the library will have low absolute abundances, which leads to stochasticity in the population dynamics and the sequencing process (Levy et al., 2015; McGee et al., 2024; Kinsler et al., 2023). Therefore, it is common to compete the mutant library by itself (case III, Figure 5A; Couce et al., 2024; Pierce et al., 2021; Wetmore et al., 2015; Price et al., 2018; Morin et al., 2018).

sec.p: A second important choice is whether to quantify fitness of a mutant relative to the whole population (‘total relative fitness’; Wetmore et al., 2015; Price et al., 2018; Morin et al., 2018) or relative to another specific genotype, like the wild-type (‘pairwise relative fitness’; see Figure 5B; Nguyen et al., 2020; Venkataram et al., 2016; Li et al., 2019; Kinsler et al., 2020; Bakerlee et al., 2021; Schmidlin et al., 2024). In the case of a mutant library growing by itself (case III), it is still possible to estimate a pairwise fitness by using a few known neutral mutants as the reference population (Couce et al., 2024; Pierce et al., 2021) and calculating fitness relative to this group (Methods; Appendix 1—section S11 and Appendix 1—section S12).

To test the consequences of these choices, we use the minimal population dynamics model (Figure 2A) parameterized by yeast single-gene knockouts and compare the estimates of total and pairwise relative fitness in bulk competitions to fitness measured in pairwise competition, which we use as the ground truth (Methods). Figure 5C shows that in bulk competitions, the error in total relative fitness (compared to fitness in pairwise competitions) is systematically offset from the error in pairwise relative fitness. For example, a mutant that grows identically to the wild-type (neutral phenotype) does not change in abundance relative to the wild-type, but it may have a net increase in its total relative abundance due to the poor growth of other mutants (compare top and bottom panel in Figure 5B). This offset affects the total relative fitness of all mutants in a uniform way (Figure 5C), such that total and pairwise relative fitness completely agree in the ranking of genotypes (Appendix 1—figure 21). Note that this offset between total and relative fitness is general and does not depend on our minimal population dynamics model (Appendix 1—section S13).

While the pairwise relative fitness is the preferred method for estimating fitness in bulk competitions, the presence of higher-order interactions means it still deviates from the fitness in pairwise competitions. Figure 5C shows the absolute error for pairwise fitness has a positive trend with fitness and increases with the relative abundance of the mutant (case III, inset in Figure 5C). For the specific population dynamics in our simulation, we decompose the higher-order interaction into two terms (Appendix 1—section S14 and Appendix 1—section S15): a fitness-independent term and a fitness-dependent term that acts as an amplifier for fitness values (Appendix 1—figure 22) and drives the positive error trend in Figure 5C. Intuitively, the population in bulk competition consumes resources more slowly and gives more time for growth rate differences to accrue. The amplification of mutant pairwise fitness in bulk is important because it widens the apparent distribution of fitness effects (leading to, for example, higher estimates for the speed of adaptation) than if fitness was measured in pairwise competition.

In order to control the error from higher-order interactions, we derive an explicit error bound. Figure 5D shows the relative error from higher-order interactions for each mutant across a range of mutant library abundances. Using the specific population dynamics of our model, we derive the following estimate: Assuming that the mutants in the library only have variation in growth rate, the mutant library abundance should satisfy(11)xlib<ϵ⋅gwt|glib−gwt|,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle x_{\mathrm{lib}} \lt {\epsilon}\cdot \frac{g_{{\mathrm{wt}}}}{|g_{\mathrm{lib}}- g_{{\mathrm{wt}}}|},$$\end{document}

where ϵ\begin{document}$\({\epsilon}\)$\end{document} is the desired threshold on the relative error (Appendix 1—figure 23), gwt\begin{document}$g_{{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} is the wild-type growth rate, and glib\begin{document}$g_{\mathrm{lib}}$\end{document} is the growth rate of the library as a whole (Appendix 1—section S16). In the case of our single-gene knockout library, Equation 11 predicts a maximum library abundance of 24.6% based on the wild-type and library growth rate (gwt=0.406\begin{document}$g_{{\mathrm{wt}}}=0.406$\end{document}, glib=0.389\begin{document}$g_{{\mathrm{lib}}}=0.389$\end{document}) for a relative error ϵ=1%\begin{document}${\epsilon}=1\%$\end{document}. Figure 5D shows that this maximum library abundance keeps the relative error below 1% for high-fitness mutants (bright yellow), because they are dominated by growth rate effects, but fails for mutants close to neutrality because they have a trade-off between growth rate and lag time, which the estimate in Equation 11 neglects. It is possible to derive a more precise bound that keeps the relative error below 1% for all mutant genotypes (in this case xlib=0.01%\begin{document}$x_{{\mathrm{lib}}}= 0.01\%$\end{document}, see vertical line in Figure 5D), but this requires prior knowledge of the trait covariation in the mutant library (Appendix 1—section S16).

sec.title: Previous benchmark experiments show deviation of bulk fitness from pairwise competition
sec.p: Our models predict that higher-order effects amplify pairwise fitness measured in bulk compared to the fitness in a pairwise competition experiment. To test this prediction, we reanalyze two published benchmark experiments of bulk fitness measurements. The first data set by van Opijnen et al., 2009 measured pairwise (1:1) and bulk competitions (xlib≈99.9%\begin{document}$x_{{\mathrm{lib}}}\approx 99.9\%$\end{document}) of 46 single-gene knockouts in Streptococcus pneumoniae using logit-encoded fitness per-generation and neutral strains as the reference group. Figure 6A shows that the fitness in bulk deviates from the diagonal, and the absolute error has a positive correlation with the underlying true fitness from pairwise competition (Appendix 1—figure 24A; Pearson r=0.40,p=0.006\begin{document}$r=0.40, p=0.006$\end{document}), similar to the pattern observed in our simulations (compare Appendix 1—figure 24A with Figure 5C, case III, and Appendix 1—figure 24B with Appendix 1—figure 23C, case III).

sec.title: Discussion
Significance of fitness quantification choices for microbial ecology and evolution
sec.p: In this work, we have introduced a conceptual framework to derive common statistics of relative fitness from three essential choices:

list-item.p: The choice of the state variable for relative abundance (encoding m).
The choice of the time scale for the change in relative abundance (Δt)
In bulk competition experiments, the choice of subpopulation that acts as the reference for relative abundance of a chosen mutant genotype (Figure 5B).

sec.p: The combination of these choices leads to a range of fitness statistics, including those commonly used in population genetics (Fisher, 1930), experimental evolution (Wiser et al., 2013; Kryazhimskiy et al., 2014; Lenski et al., 1991), and gene knockout screens (Pierce et al., 2021; Wetmore et al., 2015; Price et al., 2018; Ascensao et al., 2023; Martinson et al., 2023; Morin et al., 2018; Morin et al., 2022; van Opijnen et al., 2009).

However, as we compare these statistics in simulated competition experiments, we find that the choice of time scale can lead to different mutant rankings (Figures 2B and 4A, B), confound apparent epistasis between mutations (Figure 3B), and alter the apparent long-term trend in fitness (Figure 3F), while the choice of the reference subpopulation can lead to a systematic shift in inferred fitness values (Figure 5C). The quantitative differences between relative fitness statistics affect our ability to make evolutionary predictions. Fixation probabilities and other population genetics quantities depend on ratios of parameters defining the rates of selection, mutation, and genetic drift processes (Kimura, 1962; Patwa and Wahl, 2008). These rates must be measured in the same units. For example, in batch cultures with serial transfer, genetic drift is set by the dilution bottleneck and thus operates per-cycle (e.g., 1/N\begin{document}$1/N$\end{document} per-cycle, where N\begin{document}$\(N\)$\end{document} is the bottleneck population size). Thus, quantifying a mutation’s relative fitness s\begin{document}$\(s\)$\end{document} (equivalent to the rate of selection) per-generation and comparing to genetic drift per-cycle (Ns\begin{document}$Ns$\end{document}) would incorrectly predict the fixation probability, especially in cases where per-generation and per-cycle fitness rank mutants differently. The choice of statistic may also affect the outcome of a significance test in the context of gene essentiality tests (e.g., using log or logit with the test statistic in Wetmore et al., 2015). Since these measurements often serve as a first screen to narrow down the investigation to the top set of genes (Pierce et al., 2021; Nguyen et al., 2020), a difference in mutant ranking means the investigation might miss relevant genes because of the choice of fitness statistic.

sec.title: Best practices for quantifying mutant fitness in high-throughput experiments
sec.p: Based on these insights, we recommend the following choices for quantifying relative fitness of a mutant:

list-item.p: Use the logit encoding of relative abundance, because under the null model of logistic dynamics this linearizes the trajectory of relative abundance. Only use a different encoding if alternate, non-logistic dynamics are known.

For batch growth or any experiment with non-steady state growth, use a fixed extrinsic time scale (e.g., a single growth cycle), rather than an intrinsic time scale (e.g., the number of generations), which introduces additional variation between competitions. Only quantify fitness per-generation for experiments that are known to have steady-state growth (e.g., in a chemostat).

In bulk competition experiments, always use the pairwise fitness relative to the wild-type (by including a barcoded wild-type or by grouping neutral mutants into a virtual wild-type) because this more closely matches the relative fitness in pairwise competition.

To control the error from higher-order interactions, we recommend minimizing relative abundance of the mutant library as practically feasible. For a given error tolerance, Equation 11 gives an estimate for the maximum library abundance.

sec.p: Our recommendations agree with previous criticisms of relative fitness per-generation (Kokko, 2021; Houle et al., 2011; Wagner, 2010; Lenski, 2021) and total relative fitness (Matuszewski et al., 2016; Li et al., 2018) but differ from the standard practice in high-throughput genetic screens (Wetmore et al., 2015; Price et al., 2018; Morin et al., 2018) and many evolution experiments (Durão et al., 2021; Moger-Reischer et al., 2023), including the LTEE (Wiser et al., 2013; Lenski et al., 1991). The choice of the reference group is a well-recognized issue in high-throughput evolutionary studies, in which one first estimates a total relative fitness and then subtracts a correction based on the fitness of the wild-type (Kryazhimskiy et al., 2014; Kinsler et al., 2020; Schmidlin et al., 2024) or a mean population fitness (Levy et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2019; Ascensao et al., 2023; Bakerlee et al., 2021; Li et al., 2018). In contrast, we recommend choosing the reference group at the level of relative abundance (see Methods for a step-by-step demonstration). While researchers must ultimately choose how to quantify fitness based on the specific goals and conditions of their experiment, we believe that a more consistent adherence to the recommendations above would be valuable to the field as a whole so that fitness data from one study can be quantitatively compared to fitness from another.

sec.title: How general is the disagreement between fitness statistics in pairwise competition?
sec.p: The discrepancy in mutant ranking for relative fitness per-cycle scyclelogit\begin{document}$s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}$\end{document} and per-generation sgenlogit\begin{document}$s^{\text{logit}}_{\mathrm{gen}}$\end{document} requires positive covariation between the wild-type and mutant LFCs across a set of pairwise competition experiments. This condition is not dependent on any particular mechanism or model, although our minimal model of population dynamics (Figure 2A) demonstrates one way this covariation can occur: when mutants have lower yields and are present at sufficiently high abundances to affect wild-type LFCs (Appendix 1—figure 7).

Our model focused on the effect of resource competition on fitness discrepancies since that interaction is almost always present between microbial genotypes, providing a baseline expectation. Moreover, resource competition is likely to be the only interaction in high-throughput fitness measurements of mutants with only small genetic differences (e.g., point mutations or gene knockouts) relative to a wild-type. We expect that in cases with additional interactions between mutants and the wild-type, there will be further variation in wild-type LFCs across competitions and thus even more discrepancies between fitness statistics. For example, mutants that stimulate wild-type growth via the secretion of nutrients should create positive LFC covariation across mutants and thus be ranked differently per-cycle and per-generation. Indeed, our reanalysis of LTEE competition data shows that fitness per-cycle scyclelogit\begin{document}$s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}$\end{document} and per-generation sgenlogit\begin{document}$s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}$\end{document} (equivalent to the statistic W=1+sgenlogit\begin{document}$W=1+s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}$\end{document} used in the LTEE) disagree on the fitness ranking at almost every time point (Figure 4A) and in the first 50,000 generations overall (Figure 4B).

sec.title: How general is the deviation of bulk fitness statistics from pairwise competition experiments?
sec.p: The offset in total relative fitness (between gray and orange points in Figure 5C), equivalent to the mean library fitness (Equation S88 in Appendix 1—section S13), is independent from the population dynamics (Figure 5B, Appendix 1—section S13). In contrast, the error between pairwise fitness in bulk competition and in pairwise competition (orange points in Figure 5C) is specific to the population dynamics studied here, although it points to more general mechanisms. Specifically, we expect pairwise fitness in bulk competition to deviate from pairwise competition as soon as the mutant library is able to influence the chemical environment of the competition, for example, when a large fraction of mutants fails to complete respiration of the main carbon source and instead turns to fermentation (Molenaar et al., 2009; Sonenshein, 2007; Battjes et al., 2024), with the release of pathway intermediates like acetate that indirectly lower the pH in the growth medium (Wolfe, 2005; Tran et al., 2024).

sec.title: The choice of fitness statistic in the light of other sources of discrepancy
sec.p: Besides the conceptual choices of fitness quantification discussed in this article, experimental limitations can create discrepancies between replicate fitness measurements of the same mutant (Worthan et al., 2023; Kinsler et al., 2020; Borchert et al., 2022). For example, relative abundance measurements entail sampling uncertainties (when we sample liquid for colony counting or DNA sequencing) (Blundell and Levy, 2014; Matuszewski et al., 2016; Limdi and Baym, 2023), copy number variation (Wetmore et al., 2015; Blundell and Levy, 2014), as well as PCR jackpots and sequencing read errors (Levy et al., 2015; McGee et al., 2024; Kinsler et al., 2023). Furthermore, there will inevitably be some variation in initial conditions between replicates and fluctuations during the fitness assay (Worthan et al., 2023; Kinsler et al., 2023; Borchert et al., 2022).

sec.title: Methods
Inferring growth traits for the single-gene knockout collection in yeast
sec.p: We used a previously published data set (Warringer et al., 2003) for the single-gene knockout collection in S. cerevisiae (Giaever et al., 2002), where the authors track growth of each genotype for 47 hr in monoculture, using microwell plates with defined growth medium. We downloaded this growth curve data set from the PROPHECY database (Fernandez-Ricaud et al., 2005), choosing specifically the data set measured in Synthetic Defined medium. We last accessed the PROPHECY website (http://prophecy.lundberg.gu.se/) on March 30, 2020, but as of November 15, 2025 the website is no longer accessible. We have included a reformatted version of the data with our code repository (https://github.com/justuswfink/24FitnessQuantification, copy archived at Fink, 2026). From the raw time series of optical density, the authors subtracted a background correction based on blank wells, applied another correction for nonlinearity at high optical densities, and smoothed the growth curve to remove electrical noise (Warringer et al., 2003).

We start with the curves in the published data set (9951 curves) and apply further trimming and smoothing steps (Appendix 1—section S6). From this data, we calculate the time series of instantaneous per-capita growth rate N−1dN/dt\begin{document}$N^{-1}dN/dt$\end{document} (where N is the optical density) and identify time windows where the rate is approximately constant, which we interpret as distinct growth phases (Appendix 1—section S6). We only include curves that have a single phase of constant exponential growth followed by a stationary phase of approximately zero growth (9424 curves).

We quantify the biomass yield, maximum growth rate, and the lag time from each remaining curve as follows. First, we estimate the initial abundance Ninitial\begin{document}$N_{\mathrm{initial}}$\end{document} (average optical density over first three time points) and the final abundance Nfinal\begin{document}$N_{\mathrm{final}}$\end{document} (average optical density over stationary phase) from the growth curve. Then we calculate the biomass yield as Y=(Nfinal−Ninitial)/R(0)\begin{document}$Y = (N_{\mathrm{final}}- N_{\mathrm{initial}})/R(0)$\end{document}, where R(0)=111\begin{document}$R(0) = 111$\end{document} mM (20 g/l) is the initial concentration of glucose (assuming glucose is the single limiting resource). To estimate the maximum growth rate, we average the instantaneous growth rate over the exponential phase. Finally, we estimate the lag time from the intersection of the log initial abundance (log⁡N0\begin{document}$\log N_{0}$\end{document}) with the slope of the maximum growth rate during the exponential growth phase (Zwietering et al., 1990). We excluded curves with negative initial OD, curves with negative inferred lag times, and curves with a low quality of fit between the measured time series and a simulated curve based on the inferred trait values (R2<0.95\begin{document}$R^{2} \lt 0.95$\end{document}; see below for the model). Our final database includes trait estimates for 9195 curves, which represents 92.4% of the original data set (Warringer et al., 2003).

Each single-gene deletion strain was measured in two technical replicate growth curves, using a second plate with identical layout in the same plate reader. Some genotypes have only one estimate of the growth traits because the other replicate did not pass our filters (273 genotypes), but for most genotypes, we retain two replicate estimates in our final data set (4163 genotypes); a few genotypes even have three (2 genotypes) or four replicate estimates (54 genotypes) because these genotypes were included multiple times by the original authors (Warringer et al., 2003). From these replicates, we finally calculate the average yield, growth rate, and lag time for each genotype. The data set also contained many replicate growth curves of the wild-type strain, 374 of which passed our filters. Since wild-type traits inferred from these replicates had large variation (potentially due to measuring the wild-type across many different plates and days), we define the wild-type trait as the median, not the mean, of these replicates. Although the wild-type measurements included in this data set have large trait variation (orange dots in Appendix 1—figure 4B,C), the fact that the variation across knockouts is significantly greater than for the wild-type replicates in terms of growth rate (Levene’s test p=1.3×10−9\begin{document}$p = 1.3 \times 10^{-9}$\end{document}) and lag time (Levene’s test p=0.025\begin{document}$p=0.025$\end{document}), and that the replicate measurements of gene knockouts are correlated (Appendix 1—figure 5), suggests that these trait measurements do capture true genetic variation. In contrast, the variation in biomass yield across knockouts is not significantly different from the variation across wild-type replicates (Levene’s test p=0.44\begin{document}$p=0.44$\end{document}), suggesting that the variation in biomass yield is driven by non-genetic factors like the abundance or batch of resources used for each growth measurement.

sec.title: Simulating population dynamics in competition experiments
sec.p: Throughout this work, we model the competition between a set of genotypes during a single batch culture growth cycle using the following model of population dynamics (Manhart et al., 2018; Manhart and Shakhnovich, 2018):(12a)1NjdNjdt=gj(t,R),Nj(0)=xj(0)N0,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{1}{N_{j}}\frac{dN_{j}}{dt}= g_{j}(t, R),\qquad \quad \;\; N_{j}(0) = x_{j}(0) N_{0},$$\end{document}(12b)dRdt=−∑j1YjdNjdt,R(0)=R0,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{dR}{dt}=- \sum _{j} \frac{1}{Y_{j}}\frac{dN_{j}}{dt}, \qquad \quad \; R(0) = R_{0},$$\end{document}

where for each genotype j, Nj\begin{document}$N_{j}$\end{document} is the absolute abundance, xj(0)\begin{document}$x_{j}(0)$\end{document} the initial relative abundance, gj(t,R)\begin{document}$g_{j}(t, R)$\end{document} the growth rate, and Yj\begin{document}$Y_{j}$\end{document} the biomass yield, where the genotypes include a wild-type as well as one or more mutants. The initial absolute abundance of all genotypes together is N0\begin{document}$N_{0}$\end{document}, and the concentration of the single limiting resource is R with initial value R0\begin{document}$R_{0}$\end{document}. Note that Equation 12b assumes that cells consume resources only for biomass growth and not for maintenance of existing biomass.

To capture the sigmoidal shape of typical growth curves with a lag phase, exponential growth phase, and saturation phase (e.g., Appendix 1—figure 4A), we model the dependence of growth rate on time and resource concentration as(13)gj(t,R)=gjΘ(t−λj)Θ(R),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle g_{j}(t, R) = g_{j} \Theta (t - \lambda _{j}) \Theta (R),$$\end{document}
where Θ\begin{document}$\Theta $\end{document} is the step function:(14)Θ(z)={0z≤0,1z>0.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Theta (z) = \begin{cases} 0&z\leq 0, \\ 1&z \gt 0. \end{cases}$$\end{document}

In this model, a genotype has an initial lag phase of time λj\begin{document}$\lambda _{j}$\end{document} where no growth occurs, followed by a phase of constant exponential growth at rate gj\begin{document}$g_{j}$\end{document}, and ending when the resource concentration R\begin{document}$\(R\)$\end{document} reaches zero. The time to resource depletion, which we also call the saturation time, is defined by the implicit equation R(tsat)=0\begin{document}$R({t_{\mathrm{sat}}}) = 0$\end{document}. The simple form of the growth response (Equation 13) means that the absolute abundance of genotype j at saturation is(15)Nj(tsat)=Nj(t0)egj(tsat−λj)Θ(tsat−λj)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle N_j(t_{\mathrm{sat}}) = N_j(t_0)e^{{g_j(t_{\mathrm{sat}}-\lambda_j)}\Theta(t_{\mathrm{sat}}-\lambda_j)} $$\end{document}
and its LFC is(16)LFCj=gj(tsat−λj)Θ(tsat−λj)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathrm{LFC}_j = g_j(t_{\mathrm{sat}} - \lambda_j)\Theta(t_{\mathrm{sat}} - \lambda_j) $$\end{document}

To calculate relative fitness per-cycle (Equation 9) and per-generation (Equation 10), we numerically determine the saturation time tsat\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{sat}}}$\end{document} by integrating the biomass and resource dynamics (Equation 12) as described in previous work (Manhart et al., 2018; Manhart and Shakhnovich, 2018). We note that it is also possible to derive an approximate expression for the saturation time tsat\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{sat}}}$\end{document} which we use for our analytical calculations (Appendix 1—section S7).

sec.title: Testing epistasis between mutations in the population dynamics model
sec.p: Consider a wild-type strain with growth rate gwt=1\begin{document}${g_{\mathrm{wt}}}=1$\end{document}, lag time λwt=2\begin{document}${\lambda_{\mathrm{wt}}}=2$\end{document}, and biomass yield Ywt=1\begin{document}${Y_{\mathrm{wt}}}=1$\end{document}. We define six basic mutations that represent the six directions of the trait space in our model: a mutation that increases growth rate (gmut=1.2\begin{document}${g_{\mathrm{mut}}}= 1.2$\end{document}; symbol +g\begin{document}$+g$\end{document}), a mutation that decreases growth rate (gmut=0.8\begin{document}${g_{\mathrm{mut}}}= 0.8$\end{document}; symbol −g\begin{document}$-g$\end{document}), a mutation that increases lag time (λmut=3\begin{document}${\lambda_{\mathrm{mut}}}= 3$\end{document}; symbol +λ\begin{document}$+\lambda $\end{document}), a mutation that decreases lag time (λmut=1\begin{document}${\lambda_{\mathrm{mut}}}= 1$\end{document}; symbol −λ\begin{document}$-\lambda $\end{document}), a mutation that increases yield (Ymut=4\begin{document}${Y_{\mathrm{mut}}}=4$\end{document}; symbol +Y\begin{document}$+Y$\end{document}), and a mutation that decreases yield (Ymut=0.25\begin{document}${Y_{\mathrm{mut}}}= 0.25$\end{document}; symbol −Y\begin{document}$-Y$\end{document}).

We combine these mutations into double mutants as follows: mutations are additive at the level of traits (e.g., the double mutant (+g,−g)\begin{document}$(+g,-g)$\end{document} is neutral), and mutations in different traits are independent. For a given pair of mutations, epistasis is defined as (Krug, 2018)(17)E=s(A,B)−s(A)−s(B),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle E = s(A,B) - s(A) - s(B),$$\end{document}

where s(A)\begin{document}$s(A)$\end{document} is the relative fitness of the single mutant with mutation A, s(B)\begin{document}$s(B)$\end{document} is the relative fitness of the single mutant with mutation B, and s(A,B)\begin{document}$s(A,B)$\end{document} is the relative fitness of the double mutant with both A\begin{document}$\(A\)$\end{document} and B\begin{document}$\(B\)$\end{document}. We estimate the fitness of each mutant by simulating one growth cycle of competition with the wild-type (at initially equal abundance) using an initial biomass of N0=0.01\begin{document}$\(N_{0} = 0.01\)$\end{document} and initial resource concentration R0=0.5\begin{document}$R_{0}=0.5$\end{document}. These conditions are chosen such that mutations that increase biomass yield reach a maximum density of up to N(tsat)=2\begin{document}$N({t_{\mathrm{sat}}})=2$\end{document}, on the same scale as the optical density measured for the empirical knockouts of S. cerevisiae (Appendix 1—figure 4C).

sec.title: Quantifying total and pairwise relative fitness in bulk competition experiments
sec.p: We define total and pairwise relative fitness, two alternative measures of fitness in bulk competition experiments, as follows. Consider a population with multiple genotypes such that each genotype i\begin{document}$\(i\)$\end{document} has absolute abundance Ni(t)\begin{document}$N_{i}(t)$\end{document} at time t. The total relative abundance of the genotype is(18)xi(t)=Ni(t)∑jNj(t).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle x_{i}(t) = \frac{N_{i}(t)}{\sum _{j}N_{j}(t)}.$$\end{document}

The ‘total’ here refers to the fact that this is the abundance of genotype i\begin{document}$\(i\)$\end{document} relative to all other genotypes in the population. Similarly, we can think of the definition of relative fitness discussed in the main text (Equation 4) as the total relative fitness of this genotype under an encoding m:(19)σim=ddtm(xi(t)).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \sigma ^{m}_{i} = \frac{d }{dt}m(x_{i}(t)).$$\end{document}

However, sometimes we want to track the dynamics of a genotype relative to another specific genotype; for example, to follow the fate of a mutant against the wild-type in a bulk competition experiment. For a pair of genotypes i≠j\begin{document}$i \neq j$\end{document}, we thus define the pairwise relative abundance(20)xij(t)=xi(t)xi(t)+xj(t),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle x_{ij}(t) = \frac{x_{i}(t)}{x_{i}(t) + x_{j}(t)},$$\end{document}

which is the relative abundance of genotype i in a subpopulation of only genotypes i and j. To predict the change in the pairwise relative abundance, we can use the slope(21)sijm=ddtm(xij(t)),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{m}_{ij}= \frac{d}{dt}m(x_{ij}(t)),$$\end{document}

which defines the pairwise relative fitness of genotype i with respect to genotype j (see Appendix 1—section S12 for a generalized definition that covers the case i = j). In the special case of a population with only two strains, the pairwise relative fitness and total relative fitness are identical (σ2m=s21m\begin{document}$\sigma ^{m}_{2} = s^{m}_{21}$\end{document}), but they may differ with more than two genotypes (Appendix 1—section S13).

It is also possible to define the total and pairwise relative fitness statistics as finite differences over a time interval, rather than as instantaneous derivatives. For example, we can define them over a growth cycle starting at t=0\begin{document}$t = 0$\end{document} and ending at t=tsat\begin{document}$t = {t_{\mathrm{sat}}}$\end{document}:(22)σi,cyclem=m(xi(tsat))−m(xi(0)),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \sigma ^{m}_{i,\mathrm{cycle}} = m(x_{i}({t_\mathrm{sat}})) - m(x_{i}(0)),$$\end{document}(23)sij,cyclem=m(xij(tsat))−m(xij(0)).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s_{ij,\mathrm{cycle}}^{m} = m(x_{ij}({t_\mathrm{sat}})) - m(x_{ij}(0)).$$\end{document}

For these fitness statistics in the bulk competitions, we use the logit encoding(24)σi,cyclelogit=log⁡xi(tsat)1−xi(tsat)−log⁡xi(0)1−xi(0),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \sigma ^{{\text{logit}}}_{i,{\mathrm{cycle}}} = \log \frac{x_{i}({t_{\mathrm{sat}}})}{1-x_{i}({t_{\mathrm{sat}}})}- \log \frac{x_{i}(0)}{1-x_{i}(0)},$$\end{document}(25)sij,cyclelogit=log⁡xi(tsat)xi(0)−log⁡xj(tsat)xj(0),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s_{ij,{\mathrm{cycle}}}^{{\text{logit}}} = \log \frac{x_{i}({t_{\mathrm{sat}}})}{x_{i}(0)}- \log \frac{x_{j}({t_{\mathrm{sat}}})}{x_{j}(0)},$$\end{document}

where we have rewritten sij,cyclelogit\begin{document}$s_{ij,{\mathrm{cycle}}}^{{\operatorname{logit}}}$\end{document} in the form that it is presented in bulk competition experiments (Couce et al., 2024; Bakerlee et al., 2021; Schmidlin et al., 2024). The logit encoding has mathematical advantages for coarse-graining the relative fitness of genotype groups (Appendix 1—section S11), but using the log encoding is another common choice in the literature (Pierce et al., 2021; Johnson et al., 2019; Kinsler et al., 2020). However, the relative abundances of the individual mutants in our simulated bulk competition experiments are low enough that these two encodings are approximately equivalent (logitx≈log⁡x\begin{document}$\text{logit}\,x \approx \log x$\end{document} for x≪1\begin{document}$x\ll 1$\end{document}).

Unlike the comparison between per-cycle and per-generation relative fitness where we focused on rank differences (Figure 2B), here we can evaluate absolute differences in fitness estimates because the total and pairwise fitness in bulk fitness are measured in the same units as the relative fitness in pairwise competition. For all mutant genotypes, we calculate the absolute error between these bulk fitness estimates (Equation 24; Equation 25) and the relative fitness in pairwise competitions (Equation 9), which we take as the ground truth (Figure 5C). Note that the pairwise competition could depend on the initial relative abundance of the mutant; we have chosen a very low relative abundance (10−6) that mimics a mutant arising de novo and where this dependence is very weak.

Clearly, minimizing the abundance of the mutant library minimizes the strength of higher-order interactions (also reducing ranking disagreement, Appendix 1—figure 21B, C). As low mutant abundances create practical problems for experiments, it is valuable to identify a maximum abundance for the mutant library that keeps the error from bulk fitness estimates below a desired threshold (Equation 11). It is convenient to express this threshold in relative rather than absolute terms (compare Appendix 1—figure 23 to Figure 5C).
