sec.title: S1. Different types of fitness under example models of population dynamics
sec.p: In this section, we explicitly calculate relative fitness of a mutant under a few example models of population dynamics, using the different encodings of relative abundance as described in the main text (main text Figure 1A). Consider a competition coculture between a wild-type genotype with absolute abundance Nwt(t)\begin{document}${N_{\mathrm{wt}}}(t)$\end{document} and a mutant genotype with absolute abundance Nmut(t)\begin{document}${N_{\mathrm{mut}}}(t)$\end{document}. We can describe their dynamics according to the ordinary differential equations (ODEs)(S1)1NwtdNwtdt=gwt(t,Nwt,Nmut),1NmutdNmutdt=gmut(t,Nwt,Nmut).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \begin{array}{ll}\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{wt}}}\frac{dN_{\mathrm{wt}}}{dt} = g_{\mathrm{wt}}(t,N_{\mathrm{wt}},N_{\mathrm{mut}}), \\ \\ \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{mut}}}\frac{dN_{\mathrm{mut}}}{dt} = g_{\mathrm{mut}}(t,N_{\mathrm{wt}},N_{\mathrm{mut}}). \end{array} $$\end{document}

Note that the per-capita growth rates gwt\begin{document}$g_{\mathrm{wt}}$\end{document} and gmut\begin{document}${g_{\mathrm{mut}}}$\end{document} of each genotype can depend on both genotypes to reflect competition or other interactions. The relative abundance of the mutant genotype at time t is(S2)x(t)=Nmut(t)Nmut(t)+Nwt(t).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle x(t) = \frac{{N_{\text{mut}}}(t)}{{N_{\text{mut}}}(t) + {N_{\text{wt}}}(t)}.$$\end{document}

The dynamics of the mutant relative abundance are therefore described by(S3)dxdt=[gmut(t,Nwt,Nmut)−gwt(t,Nwt,Nmut)]×x(1−x).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{dx}{dt} = \left[ g_{\mathrm{mut}}(t,N_{\mathrm{wt}},N_{\mathrm{mut}}) - g_{\mathrm{wt}}(t,N_{\mathrm{wt}},N_{\mathrm{mut}}) \right] \times x(1-x).$$\end{document}

As defined in the main text (Equation 4), the relative fitness of a mutant is sm=dm/dt\begin{document}$s^{m} = dm/dt$\end{document} for an encoding m(x)\begin{document}$m(x)$\end{document} of the relative abundance x. Under the trivial linear encoding (m(x)=x\begin{document}$m(x) = x$\end{document}), the relative fitness is therefore just the right-hand side of the relative abundance ODE (Equation S3):(S4)slinear=dxdt=[gmut(t,Nwt,Nmut)−gwt(t,Nwt,Nmut)]×x(1−x).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl}s^{{\text{linear}}}&=&\frac{dx}{dt}\\&=&\bigg[{g_{\text{mut}}}(t,{N_{\text{wt}}},{N_{\text{mut}}})-{g_{\text{wt}}}(t,{N_{\text{wt}}},{N_{\text{mut}}})\bigg]\times\\&&x(1-x).\end{array}$$\end{document}

For the log encoding m(x)=log⁡x\begin{document}$m(x) = \log x$\end{document}, we use the identity dlog⁡x/dt=x−1dx/dt\begin{document}$d\log x/dt = x^{-1}dx/dt$\end{document} to obtain the log-encoded relative fitness:(S5)slog=dlog⁡xdt=[gmut(t,Nwt,Nmut)−gwt(t,Nwt,Nmut)]×(1−x).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl}s^{{\text{log}}}&=&\frac{d\log x}{dt}\\&=&\bigg[{g_{\text{mut}}}(t,{N_{\text{wt}}},{N_{\text{mut}}})-{g_{\text{wt}}}(t,{N_{\text{wt}}},{N_{\text{mut}}})\bigg]\times\\&& (1-x).\end{array}$$\end{document}

Finally, for the logit encoding m(x)=logitx=log⁡(x/(1−x))\begin{document}$m(x) = {\text{logit}}\,x = \log (x/(1-x))$\end{document}, we use the identity dlogitx/dt=x−1(1−x)−1dx/dt\begin{document}$d\,{\text{logit}}\,x/dt = x^{-1}(1-x)^{-1}dx/dt$\end{document} to obtain the logit-encoded relative fitness:(S6)slogit=ddtlogitx=gmut(t,Nwt,Nmut)−gwt(t,Nwt,Nmut).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl} s^{\text{logit}} &=& \dfrac{d}{dt} {\rm logit} \,{x} \\[6pt] &=& g_{\text{mut}}(t,N_{\text{wt}},N_{\text{mut}}) - g_{\text{wt}}(t,N_{\text{wt}},N_{\text{mut}}). \end{array} $$\end{document}

By comparing relative fitness values under the linear encoding (Equation S4) and under the logit encoding (Equation S6), we see how the logit encoding has removed the explicit dependence on the mutant relative abundance (factors of x\begin{document}$x$\end{document} and 1−x\begin{document}$1 - x$\end{document}), although there can be implicit dependence on the mutant relative abundance within the per-capita growth rates of each strain (gwt\begin{document}${g_{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} and gmut\begin{document}${g_{\mathrm{mut}}}$\end{document}) due to density-dependent growth rates.

If the per-capita growth rates gwt\begin{document}${g_{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} and gmut\begin{document}${g_{\mathrm{mut}}}$\end{document} (Equation S1) are constants, then these constant growth rates also act as fitness potentials since they each depend only on a single genotype, but their difference determines relative fitness (under the logit encoding, Equation S6) between the genotypes. The growth rate is not a fitness potential under more complex dynamics, however. For example, consider a competition model with explicit density dependence:(S7)1NwtdNwtdt=rwt(1−NwtKwt−NmutKmut),1NmutdNmutdt=rmut(1−NwtKwt−NmutKmut),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \begin{array}{c} \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{wt}}}\frac{dN_{\mathrm{wt}}}{dt} = r_{\mathrm{wt}}\left( 1-\frac{N_{\mathrm{wt}}}{K_{\mathrm{wt}}} -\frac{N_{\mathrm{mut}}}{K_{\mathrm{mut}}} \right), \\[10pt] \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{mut}}}\frac{dN_{\mathrm{mut}}}{dt} = r_{\mathrm{mut}}\left( 1-\frac{N_{\mathrm{wt}}}{K_{\mathrm{wt}}} -\frac{N_{\mathrm{mut}}}{K_{\mathrm{mut}}} \right), \end{array} $$\end{document}

where the growth rates decrease as the genotype abundances reach their carrying capacities Kwt\begin{document}$K_{\mathrm{wt}}$\end{document} and Kmut\begin{document}$K_{\mathrm{mut}}$\end{document}, and the maximum growth rates at low abundances are rwt\begin{document}$r_{{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} and rmut\begin{document}$r_{{\mathrm{mut}}}$\end{document}. In this case, the relative fitness under the logit encoding is (from Equation S6)(S8)slogit=(rmut−rwt)(1−NwtKwt−NmutKmut).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{{\rm{logit}}}= (r_{{\text{mut}}} - r_{{\text{wt}}}) \left (1 - \frac{{N_{\text{wt}}}}{K_{\text{wt}}}- \frac{{N_{\text{mut}}}}{K_{\text{mut}}}\right).$$\end{document}
In this case, there is no fitness potential because it is not possible to separate Equation S8 into a difference between terms that only depend on each genotype separately.

sec.title: S2. Definition of absolute fitness for a genotype
sec.p: Here we give an explicit definition of a genotype’s absolute fitness, analogous to the definition of relative fitness in the main text (Equations 1–4). Conceptually, absolute fitness is any number that is sufficient to predict a genotype’s absolute abundance N over a short time window. Let an encoding m(N)\begin{document}$m(N)$\end{document} be any smooth, strictly increasing function of the absolute abundance N. We can then predict the absolute abundance over a time window Δt\begin{document}$\Delta t$\end{document} using a linear expansion of the encoded abundance (analogous to main text Equation 3 for relative fitness):(S9)m(N(t+Δt))≈m(N(t))+amΔt,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle m(N(t + \Delta t)) \approx m(N(t)) + a^{m}\Delta t,$$\end{document}
where(S10)am=dmdt\begin{document}$$\displaystyle a^m=\frac{dm}{dt}$$\end{document}

is defined as the absolute fitness of the genotype under the encoding m\begin{document}$\(m\)$\end{document} (analogous to main text Equation 4 for relative fitness; see also main text Figure 1B). For example, the absolute fitness of a genotype under the log encoding m(N)=log⁡N\begin{document}$\(m(N) = \log N\)$\end{document} is the per-capita growth rate:(S11)alog=1NdNdt.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle a^{\log }= \frac{1}{N}\frac{dN}{dt}.$$\end{document}

In general, the ideal encoding of absolute abundance is the inverse function of the absolute abundance trajectory N(t)\begin{document}$N(t)$\end{document} (up to a shift and rescaling), so that the first-order expansion in Equation S9 is exact and the absolute fitness am\begin{document}$\(a^{m}\)$\end{document} is sufficient to determine changes in absolute abundance up to any future time. The log encoding m(N)=log⁡N\begin{document}$m(N) = \log N$\end{document} is therefore ideal when absolute abundance grows or decays exponentially at a constant rate, while the logit encoding m(N)=logitN\begin{document}$m(N) = {\operatorname{logit}}\,N$\end{document} is ideal for a population that grows with logistic density dependence (Equation S7 in case of a single genotype).

Absolute fitness and relative fitness are related since the relative abundance of a genotype is determined by normalizing its absolute abundance by the absolute abundance of all genotypes in the population. Specifically, the relative fitness of a genotype is determined by the absolute fitnesses for all genotypes in the population. For example, in the case of two genotypes, the relative fitness under the logit encoding (Equation S6) is the difference between the genotypes' absolute fitness under the log encoding (Equation S11). In the case of constant per-capita growth rates, these log-encoded absolute fitnesses also act as fitness potentials.

sec.title: S3. The role of logistic population dynamics in logit-encoded relative fitness
sec.p: Here we show how the logit encoding of relative abundance is related to the logistic model of population dynamics. For a relative abundance x\begin{document}$\(x\)$\end{document}, logistic dynamics are(S12)dxdt=rx(1−x),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{dx}{dt}= r x (1-x),$$\end{document}

where r\begin{document}$\(r\)$\end{document} is the exponential rate at which relative abundance increases from low values. This form emerges from the general dynamics of relative abundance (Equation S3) when the difference in per-capita growth rates gmut\begin{document}${g_{\mathrm{mut}}}$\end{document} and gwt\begin{document}${g_{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} is constant. One can also interpret the logistic model as a lowest-order approximation for more complex dynamics. That is, consider a general equation for relative abundance:(S13)dxdt=f(x),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{dx}{dt}= f(x),$$\end{document}

for an arbitrary function f(x)\begin{document}$\(f(x)\)$\end{document}. Since this function must obey the boundary conditions f(0)=0\begin{document}$f(0) = 0$\end{document} and f(1)=0\begin{document}$f(1) = 0$\end{document} (the relative abundance must stop changing when it either goes extinct or fixes), a polynomial expansion of f(x)\begin{document}$f(x)$\end{document} must have roots at these values:(S14)f(x)=rx(1−x)(1+O(x)).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle f(x) = rx(1 - x)(1 + \mathcal{O}(x)).$$\end{document}
Thus, the logistic model in Equation S12 is a lowest-order approximation even when the true dynamics are more complex.
The logistic differential equation in Equation S12 has the solution(S15)x(t)=x(0)ertx(0)ert+1−x(0).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle x(t) = \frac{x(0)e^{rt}}{x(0)e^{rt}+ 1 - x(0)}.$$\end{document}

The logit encoding of the logistic relative abundance has linear dependence on time:(S16)m(x)=logitx=rt+log⁡(1−x(0)x(0)).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl}m(x)&=&{\text{logit}}\,x\\&=&rt+\log\left(\frac{1-x(0)}{x(0)}\right).\end{array}$$\end{document}

This is another way to see why the relative fitness under the logit encoding (the time derivative of Equation S16) is constant under logistic dynamics. Mathematically, this occurs because the logit function is the inverse of the logistic dynamics (Equation S15), up to a shift and rescaling. Thus, if the relative abundance dynamics are different from logistic (Equation S12), the logit encoding no longer exactly linearizes the trajectory of relative abundance and thus is no longer the optimal encoding for relative fitness (see Appendix 1—figure 2 and the mathematical notes by Mallet, 2012 for more examples).

More generally, the ideal encoding for a given relative abundance dynamics x(t)\begin{document}$x(t)$\end{document} is any linear function of the inverse m(x(t))=at(x)+b\begin{document}$m(x(t))=at(x)+b$\end{document} of those dynamics. Note that the ambiguous scale includes log and logit encodings with a different base of the logarithm (discussed by Chevin, 2011). The inversion of x(t)\begin{document}$x(t)$\end{document} is equivalent to removing frequency (relative abundance) dependence from the relative fitness statistic sm\begin{document}$s^m$\end{document}(Levin, 1988).

sec.title: S4. Relative fitness predictions in discrete time: additive versus multiplicative form
sec.p: In our framework, relative fitness is a statistic that predicts relative abundance in an additive equation (main text Equation 3) but sometimes the dynamics of individual genotypes are modeled using a multiplicative form of fitness. In this section, we show how these multiplicative fitness statistics are related to the additive fitness statistics, in particular for the logit encoding.

We consider a population of a wild-type and a mutant genotype, where we track the mutant’s relative abundance over multiple rounds of competition (e.g., growth cycles)(S17)x(0)→x(1)→⋯→x(r−1)→x(r)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle x(0) \to x(1) \to \dots \to x(r-1) \to x(r)$$\end{document}
and the variable x\begin{document}$\(x\)$\end{document} changes each round according to some underlying population dynamics.

In a modeling approach typical to many studies in population genetics (Krug, 2018), these population dynamics are captured in the genotype-specific growth factors(S18)fmut=Nmut(r+1)Nmut(r),fwt=Nwt(r+1)Nwt(r)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle f_{\text{mut}} = \frac{N_{\text{mut}}(r+1)}{N_{\text{mut}}(r)}, \qquad f_{\text{wt}} = \frac{N_{\text{wt}}(r+1)}{N_{\text{wt}}(r)} $$\end{document}

which determine the update equation for the mutant relative abundance(S19)x(r+1)=x(r)fmut(1−x(r))fwt+x(r)fmut\begin{document}$$\displaystyle x(r+1) = \frac{x(r)f_{\mathrm{mut}}}{(1-x(r))f_{\mathrm{wt}} + x(r)f_{\mathrm{mut}}} $$\end{document}

which is the discrete-time analogue to a differential equation (Equation S1). We divide Equation S19 by 1−x(r+1)\begin{document}$\(1-x(r+1)\)$\end{document} to obtain the form(S20)x(r+1)1−x(r+1)=x(r)1−x(r)fmutfwt\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{x(r+1)}{1-x(r+1)} = \frac{x(r)}{1-x(r)}\frac{f_{\mathrm{mut}}}{f_{\mathrm{wt}}} $$\end{document}

which allows us to recognize the ratio of growth factors fmut/fwt\begin{document}$f_{{\mathrm{mut}}}/f_{{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} as a relative fitness statistic, since it is sufficient to predict the relative abundance of the mutant genotype (under the encoding m(x)=x/(1−x)\begin{document}$m(x) = x/(1-x)$\end{document}). But the statistic fmut/fwt\begin{document}$f_{{\mathrm{mut}}}/f_{{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} acts as a multiplying factor in Equation S20, whereas the general form of relative fitness sm\begin{document}$\(s^{m}\)$\end{document} (main text Equation 3) acts as an additive factor. What is the relationship between the multiplicative and the additive form of discrete-time relative fitness statistics?

To describe discrete rounds of population dynamics in our framework, we treat the relative abundance x(r)\begin{document}$\(x(r)\)$\end{document} as samples from a continuous time series, separated by a time-gap Δt=t(r+1)−t(r)\begin{document}$\Delta t = t(r+1) - t(r)$\end{document}. For a chosen encoding m, the relative abundance of the mutant genotype in the future round is predicted by(S21)m(x(r+1))=m(x(r))+smΔt\begin{document}$$\displaystyle m(x(r+1)) = m(x(r)) + s^{m} \Delta t$$\end{document}

since this is how we defined relative fitness sm\begin{document}$s^{m}$\end{document} in main text Equation 3. This relative fitness acts as an additive factor, but we apply the exponential function on both sides of Equation S21 to obtain the updated equation(S22)exp⁡[m(x(r+1))]=exp⁡[m(x(r))]⋅exp⁡(smΔt),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \exp \left [m(x(r+1))\right ] = \exp \left [m(x(r))\right ] \cdot \exp (s^{m} \Delta t),$$\end{document}

where the additive fitness slogit\begin{document}$s^{{\text{logit}}}$\end{document} together with the time scale Δt\begin{document}$\Delta t$\end{document} acts as a multiplicative factor. Specifically for the logit encoding m(x)=logitx\begin{document}$m(x) = {\text{logit}}\,x$\end{document} we have(S23)x(r+1)1−x(r+1)=x(r)1−x(r)exp⁡(slogitΔt).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{x(r+1)}{1 - x(r+1)}= \frac{x(r)}{1-x(r)}\exp (s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}\Delta t).$$\end{document}

We compare Equation S23 to Equation S20 and solve for the relative fitness of the mutant genotype(S24)slogit=log⁡fmut−log⁡fwtΔt,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{\mathrm{logit}} = \frac{\log f_{\mathrm{mut}} - \log f_{\mathrm{wt}}}{\Delta t} ,$$\end{document}

as a function of the growth factors fmut,fwt\begin{document}$f_{{\mathrm{mut}}}, f_{{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document}. Using the definition of the growth factors (Equation S18), we see that Equation S24 is simply the discrete-time relative fitness for the logit encoding in terms of the mutant and wild-type log fold-change (LFC; main text Equation 8). As a general point, we note that the growth-factor fmut\begin{document}$f_{{\mathrm{mut}}}$\end{document} qualifies as an absolute fitness (since it is sufficient to predict the absolute abundance N(r+1)\begin{document}$N(r+1)$\end{document}), but does not constitute a relative fitness statistic (since we also need to know fwt\begin{document}$f_{{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document}, see Equation S20 or Equation S24).

More generally, for a given encoding function m(x)\begin{document}$m(x)$\end{document} we define the mutant’s multiplicative relative fitness over a discrete growth cycle as(S25)wm=exp⁡(smΔt)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle w^{m} = \exp (s^{m} \Delta t)$$\end{document}

where sm\begin{document}$\(s^{m}\)$\end{document} is the additive relative fitness for this growth-cycle under the chosen encoding (main text Equation 4) and Δt\begin{document}$\(\Delta t\)$\end{document} is the duration of the growth-cycle in time units that match sm\begin{document}$s^{m}$\end{document}. Equation S25 shows that the additive fitness sm\begin{document}$\(s^{m}\)$\end{document} has time units, but the multiplicative fitness does not and is formally a dimensionless quantity. These dimensionless units are preserved in the approximate formula(S26)wm≈1+smΔt,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle w^{m} \approx 1 + s^{m} \Delta t,$$\end{document}

which is the first-order expansion of Equation S25 in the limit of weak selection (|smΔt|≪1\begin{document}$|s^{m}\Delta t|\ll 1$\end{document}). For example, if we choose to measure relative fitness with the logit encoding on the time scale per-cycle (Δt=1 cycle\begin{document}$\Delta t = 1\ {\mathrm{cycle}}$\end{document}), we get(S27)wlogit≈1+scyclelogit⋅1 cycle\begin{document}$$\displaystyle w^{{\text{logit}}}\approx 1 + s^{{\text{logit}}}_{{\mathrm{cycle}}}\cdot 1\ {\mathrm{cycle}}$$\end{document}

which is the same multiplicative fitness as if we choose to measure the relative fitness on the time scale per-generation (Δt=LFCwt\begin{document}$\Delta t = {\mathrm{LFC}}^{{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document}):(S28)wlogit≈1+sgenlogitLFCwt.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle w^{{\operatorname{logit}}}\approx 1 + {s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}{\mathrm{LFC}}^{{\mathrm{wt}}}.$$\end{document}
In both cases, the time units for the discrete-time additive fitness cancel in the product term.

So how would a mutant ranking in the multiplicative fitness wlogit\begin{document}$\(w^{{\operatorname{logit}}}\)$\end{document} rank a set of mutant genotypes compared to the fitness statistics scyclelogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}}$\end{document} or sgenlogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document}? Equation S27 shows that the multiplicative fitness statistic wlogit\begin{document}$\(w^{{\operatorname{logit}}}\)$\end{document} agrees with the relative fitness per-cycle slogit\begin{document}$\(s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}\)$\end{document}, but can differ from the ranking in the relative fitness per-generation sgencycle\begin{document}${s^{{\mathrm{cycle}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document} as both terms of the product in Equation S28 depend on the mutant.

Finally, we address the question of how the relative fitness scyclelogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}}$\end{document} agrees in the ranking with the multiplicative fitness wlogit\begin{document}$\(w^{{\operatorname{logit}}}\)$\end{document}, but disagrees with the fitness statistic defined in the Long-Term Evolution Experiment (Lenski et al., 1991) as(S29)W=1+sgenlogit.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle W = 1 + {s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}.$$\end{document}

By comparing Equation S29 to the multiplicative fitness in Equation S26, we see that the LTEE fitness statistic W does not derive from the general form of the multiplicative fitness (Equation S25) as all statistics derived from this approximation have a multiplying factor Δt\begin{document}$\(\Delta t\)$\end{document} that cancels the units of time in sm\begin{document}$\(s^{m}\)$\end{document}. The fact that the LTEE fitness statistic W\begin{document}$\(W\)$\end{document} (Equation S29) misses the term LFCwt\begin{document}${\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} compared to the logit-based multiplicative fitness wlogit\begin{document}$\(w^{{\operatorname{logit}}}\)$\end{document} (Equation S28) means that the objects have different units of time and different rankings.

sec.title: S5. Derivation of mismatch conditions for relative fitness per-cycle and per-generation
sec.p: In this section, we derive the conditions for a ranking mismatch between the relative fitness per-cycle and per-generation (for the logit-encoded relative abundance) across a set of competition experiments. Consider a batch culture where a competing wild-type and mutant genotype have log fold-changes LFCwt\begin{document}${\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} and LFCmut\begin{document}${\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{mut}}}$\end{document} over a single growth cycle. The LFCs are convenient variables to describe these dynamics since we can express the mutant’s relative fitness per-cycle as (main text Equation 9)(S30)scyclelogit=LFCmut−LFCwt\begin{document}$$\displaystyle {s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}}= {\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{mut}}}- {\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{wt}}}$$\end{document}

and the mutant’s relative fitness per-generation as (main text Equation 10)(S31)sgenlogit=LFCmutLFCwt−1.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle {s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}= \frac{{\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{mut}}}}{{\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{wt}}}}- 1.$$\end{document}
Here, we assume both LFCs are nonzero (so that measuring fitness per-generation is meaningful; see discussion in main text).

To determine how these two fitness statistics lead to different rankings, we consider two competition experiments A and B, which may represent two different mutants competing against the same wild-type or the same mutant tested in two different environments. A mismatch in ranking occurs when the fitness per-cycle in competition is higher in B, while the fitness per-generation is higher in A:(S32)scyclelogit(LFCwtB,LFCmutB)>scyclelogit(LFCwtA,LFCmutA),sgenlogit(LFCwtB,LFCmutB)<sgenlogit(LFCwtA,LFCmutA).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl}{s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}}({\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{wt}}}^{B},{\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{mut}}}^{B})&\gt&{s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}}({\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{wt}}}^{A},{\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{mut}}}^{A}),\\ {s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}({\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{wt}}}^{B},{\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{mut}}}^{B})&\lt&{s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}({\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{wt}}}^{A},{\mathrm{LFC}}_{{\mathrm{mut}}}^{A}).\end{array}$$\end{document}

We insert the expressions for relative fitness per-cycle (Equation S30) and per-generation (Equation S31) into Equation S32 to rewrite the condition for ranking mismatch in terms of the LFCs:(S33a)LFCmutB>LFCwtB+(LFCmutA−LFCwtA),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathrm{LFC}_{\mathrm{mut}}^{B} \gt \mathrm{LFC}_{\mathrm{wt}}^{B} + \left( \mathrm{LFC}_{\mathrm{mut}}^{A} - \mathrm{LFC}_{\mathrm{wt}}^{A} \right),$$\end{document}(S33b)LFCmutB<LFCwtB⋅LFCmutALFCwtA.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathrm{LFC}_{\mathrm{mut}}^{B} \lt \mathrm{LFC}_{\mathrm{wt}}^{B} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{LFC}_{\mathrm{mut}}^{A}} {\mathrm{LFC}_{\mathrm{wt}}^{A}}.$$\end{document}

For a given competition A\begin{document}$A$\end{document}, Equation S33a and Equation S33b define an area in the space of LFCs where competition B\begin{document}$B$\end{document} can lie such that competitions' fitness is ranked differently per-cycle versus per-generation (main text Figure 1D shows an example as the red-shaded area). Biologically, these constraints describe a situation where the mutant and wild-type LFCs are both higher or both lower in competition B than in competition A (i.e., so that the gray point is up and to the right of the red point in Figure 1D, or down and to the left), but the LFC differences must be sufficiently balanced between the mutant and wild-type (i.e., so that the point lies within the red area in Figure 1D).

Typically, however, the LFCs of the wild-type and the mutant are not independent, since these LFCs are jointly constrained by the fact both strains compete for the same finite resources. For example, assume that a single limiting resource with concentration R is consumed in proportion to the growth of each genotype’s biomass according to(S34)dRdt=−1YwtdNwtdt−1YmutdNmutdt,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{dR}{dt}= -\frac{1}{{Y_{\mathrm{wt}}}}\frac{d{N_{\mathrm{wt}}}}{dt}- \frac{1}{{Y_{\mathrm{mut}}}}\frac{d{N_{\mathrm{mut}}}}{dt},$$\end{document}

where Ywt\begin{document}${Y_{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} and Ymut\begin{document}${Y_{\mathrm{mut}}}$\end{document} are the wild-type and mutant biomass yields (stoichiometry of biomass to resource). We can integrate Equation S34 to obtain(S35)R(t)=R(0)−Nwt(t)−Nwt(0)Ywt−Nmut(t)−Nmut(0)Ymut.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle R(t) = R(0) - \frac{N_{\mathrm{wt}}(t) - N_{\mathrm{wt}}(0)}{Y_{\mathrm{wt}}} - \frac{N_{\mathrm{mut}}(t) - N_{\mathrm{mut}}(0)}{Y_{\mathrm{mut}}}. $$\end{document}

The growth cycle stops when no resource remains (R(t)=0\begin{document}$R(t) = 0$\end{document}), such that(S36)R(0)+Nwt(0)Ywt+Nmut(0)Ymut=Nwt(0)eLFCwtYwt+Nmut(0)eLFCmutYmut\begin{document}$$\displaystyle R(0) + \frac{N_{\mathrm{wt}}(0)}{Y_{\mathrm{wt}}} + \frac{N_{\mathrm{mut}}(0)}{Y_{\mathrm{mut}}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{wt}}(0)e^{\mathrm{LFC}_{\mathrm{wt}}}}{Y_{\mathrm{wt}}} + \frac{N_{\mathrm{mut}}(0)e^{\mathrm{LFC}_{\mathrm{mut}}}}{Y_{\mathrm{mut}}} $$\end{document}

where we have expressed the genotype abundances at the end of the growth cycle in terms of their LFCs. Equation S36 thus entails a constraint between the wild-type and mutant LFCs. For a set of mutant competitions with the same initial resource concentration R(0)\begin{document}$R(0)$\end{document}, initial abundances Nwt(0)\begin{document}${N_{\mathrm{wt}}}(0)$\end{document} and Nmut(0)\begin{document}${N_{\mathrm{mut}}}(0)$\end{document}, and yields Ywt\begin{document}${Y_{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} and Ymut\begin{document}${Y_{\mathrm{mut}}}$\end{document}, the mutant and wild-type LFCs are constrained by Equation S36 to fall along a one-dimensional curve (black line in Appendix 1—figure 3A). Geometrically, we see that this constraint on LFCs is incompatible with the requirements for a ranking mismatch between fitness per-cycle and per-generation for a pair of mutant competitions (compare black line and red shaded areas in Appendix 1—figure 3A). However, if some mutant competitions deviate from this constraint, for example by having different yields Ymut\begin{document}${Y_{\mathrm{mut}}}$\end{document} or initial conditions Nwt(0)\begin{document}${N_{\text{wt}}}(0)$\end{document} and Nmut(0)\begin{document}${N_{\text{mut}}}(0)$\end{document}, then ranking mismatches may be possible (Appendix 1—figure 3B).

sec.title: S6. Analysis of growth curves to identify growth phases
sec.p: In this section, we describe in more detail how we identify growth phases from the original data set of growth curves and use this to choose a subset of curves that matches the simplified growth dynamics of our population dynamics model (Appendix 1—figure 4A). As mentioned in the main text (Methods), we downloaded this original data from the PROPHECY database (http://prophecy.lundberg.gu.se/), downloading specifically the data set for growth in Synthetic Defined medium as first analyzed and reported by Warringer et al., 2003. We last accessed the PROPHECY website (http://prophecy.lundberg.gu.se/) on March 30, 2020, but as of November 15, 2025 the website is no longer accessible. We have included a reformatted version of the data with our code repository (https://github.com/justuswfink/24FitnessQuantification, copy archived at Fink, 2026). The original growth curve data is already corrected for background and instrument non-linearities (Warringer et al., 2003) (summarized in Methods), but we decided to apply additional corrections as follows: To begin with, we concatenate the original 51 data files (for different plate reader runs) into a single, consecutive dataframe and manually handle a duplication in one of the files (Experiment No. 18). This file has no measurements for the first time point (t=0\begin{document}$t=0$\end{document}) due to a technical error in the original data export (Warringer et al., 2003), and for curves from this experimental run, we set the initial time point to NAN value in Python, meaning that these points will be ignored for any subsequent calculations of averages. More generally, we decided to trim the first four time points of all growth curves (equivalent to 1 hr 20 min from 47 hr total) and remove OD measurement below a noise threshold (OD=0.001\begin{document}$\mathrm{OD}= 0.001$\end{document}) as this improves the quality of the fit later on.

After pre-processing, we estimate a smooth time series for the instantaneous growth rate in each growth curve, using a previously published script gaussianprocess.py by Swain et al., 2016 that implements the Gaussian Process approach to smoothing (downloaded from https://swainlab.bio.ed.ac.uk/software.html). We apply this script to the logarithmic absolute abundance logOD\begin{document}$\rm log\, OD$\end{document}, and reconstruct a smoothed trajectory f(t)≈log⁡OD(t)\begin{document}$f(t)\approx \log \mathrm{OD}(t)$\end{document} as well as the first derivative df/dt\begin{document}$df/dt$\end{document} and the second derivative d2f/dt2\begin{document}$d^2f/dt^2$\end{document} (Swain et al., 2016). Effectively, the script estimates three hyperparameters that capture the shape of each curve, and we find that the estimation works best if we constrain the parameter ranges as outlined in Appendix 1—table 1.

sec.p: With a smoothed time series at hand, we now identify ‘plateaus’ of constant growth rate using the functions available in Scipy (Virtanen et al., 2020). For each growth curve, we start by identifying so-called ‘plateau seeds’, which are small intervals where the second derivative is below a chosen threshold d2f/dt2<5⋅10−6\begin{document}$d^{2} f/dt^{2} \lt 5\cdot 10^{-6}$\end{document}. For each plateau seed k in the growth curve, we calculate the average growth rate g^k\begin{document}$\hat {g}_{k}$\end{document} in the time window of the plateau. Due to some noise in the second derivative, we find many plateau seeds that are adjacent and need to be merged. To do so, we iterate over the plateau seeds in the growth curve and merge the current candidate k with the previous plateau k − 1, except one of the following conditions is true:

list-item.p: Both plateau seeds have a duration that is too long (equal to or greater than 100 min).
The transition time between the plateau seeds is too large (equal to or greater than 200 min).

The first plateau has a significantly different growth rate than the second one, such that the following equation is satisfied(S37)|gk−1−gk|>0.001+|gk|⋅0.4,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle |g_{k-1}- g_{k}| \gt 0.001 + |g_{k}|\cdot 0.4,$$\end{document}
where gk,gk−1\begin{document}$g_{k},g_{k-1}$\end{document} are the average growth rates in each plateau (per minute).

sec.p: Empirically, we find that the duration of these merged plateaus is shorter than what one would expect from visually inspecting the growth curve. Therefore, we extend the remaining plateaus in each growth curve as follows: For each plateau, we estimate the lower and upper growth rates df/dt\begin{document}$\(df/dt\)$\end{document} in the time window and take this as a growth rate corridor. We extend the plateau to the left until df/dt\begin{document}$\(df/dt\)$\end{document} leaves that growth rate corridor, and similarly extend to the right. By definition, the resulting plateau is equal to or larger than the original time window, and we recalculate the average growth rate over the time window.

From this analysis, we obtain a list of growth phases for each curve that allows us to choose a subset of curves that match our model of population dynamics (Methods). We only choose curves that have two plateaus, where the first plateau has significant growth (exponential phase), and the second plateau has no growth (stationary phase). Here, we define significant growth as the average growth rate in the plateau time window being larger than or equal to 0.0011 per minute. This forms the set of growth curves that we use to estimate growth traits (9424 curves).

sec.title: S7. The saturation time in our model of population dynamics
sec.p: In this section, we restate an explicit expression for the saturation time tsat\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{sat}}}$\end{document} in pairwise competition that was derived in earlier work and allows us to see how mutants can influence resource depletion and the wild-type LFC (main text Equation 16). Using the same model of population dynamics (Methods, main text Equation 12a), previous work (Manhart et al., 2018; Manhart and Shakhnovich, 2018) derived an approximate formula for tsat\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{sat}}}$\end{document} that shows how it depends on the underlying parameters:(S38)tsat≈λ¯+τ¯LFC,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle t_{\text{sat}} \approx \bar{\lambda} + \bar{\tau}\text{LFC},$$\end{document}
where(S39)λ¯=τ¯Y¯∑jxjgjλjYj\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \bar {\lambda }= {\bar{\tau}}{\bar{Y}}\sum _{j} \frac{x_{j} g_{j}\lambda _{j}}{Y_{j}}$$\end{document}
is the effective lag time of the population,(S40)τ¯=[∑jxjgjY¯Yj]−1\begin{document}$$\displaystyle {\bar{\tau}}= \left [\sum _{j} x_{j}g_{j}\frac{{\bar{Y}}}{Y_{j}}\right ]^{-1}$$\end{document}

is the effective e\begin{document}$\(e\)$\end{document}-fold growth time (reciprocal exponential growth rate) of the population,(S41)Y¯=[∑jxjYj]−1\begin{document}$$\displaystyle {\bar{Y}}= \left [\sum _{j} \frac{x_{j}}{Y_{j}}\right ]^{-1}$$\end{document}
is the effective yield of the population, and(S42)LFC=log⁡(1+R0Y¯N0)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle {\text{LFC}}= \log \left (1 + \frac{R_{0}{\bar{Y}}}{N_{0}}\right)$$\end{document}

is the log fold-change of the total biomass, which depends on the initial absolute abundance N0\begin{document}$N_{0}$\end{document} of all genotypes and the initial concentration of resources R0\begin{document}$R_{0}$\end{document}.

Equation S38 shows how each competing genotype influences the saturation time tsat\begin{document}${t_{\rm{sat}}}$\end{document} and thus the LFCs of all other genotypes via main text Equation 16. For example, adding a mutant with a slow growth rate increases the effective doubling time (Equation S40), while a mutant with a long lag time will increase the effective lag time (Equation S39). Genotypes also influence the saturation time (Equation S38) through the effective yield Y¯\begin{document}$\bar {Y}$\end{document}, which is the harmonic average of yields for all genotypes (Equation S41). The harmonic average means that adding mutants with low biomass yield Yj\begin{document}$Y_{j}$\end{document} can significantly shorten the saturation time, but mutants that are more efficient (high Yj\begin{document}$\(Y_{j}\)$\end{document}) have little influence on the duration of the growth cycle. Note that genotypes must be at sufficiently high relative abundance to significantly influence the effective population traits, since the contribution of each genotype j is weighted by its relative abundance xj\begin{document}$x_{j}$\end{document}.

For bulk competition experiments, the saturation time of the culture can be expressed as an interpolation between the traits of the wild-type and the mutant library. We rewrite Equations S39 and S40 as a function of mutant library traits(S43)λ¯=τ¯Y¯((1−xlib)gwtλwtYwt+xlibglibλlibYlib),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \bar{\lambda} = \bar{\tau} \bar{Y} \left( (1 - x_{\text{lib}}) \frac{g_{\text{wt}} \lambda_{\text{wt}}}{Y_{\text{wt}}} + x_{\text{lib}} \frac{g_{\text{lib}} \lambda_{\text{lib}}}{Y_{\text{lib}}} \right),$$\end{document}(S44)τ¯=((1−xlib)gwtY¯Ywt+xlibglibY¯Ylib)−1,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle {\bar{\tau}}= \left ((1 - x_{{\text{lib}}})g_{{\text{wt}}} \frac{\bar {Y}}{Y_{{\text{wt}}}}+ x_{{\text{lib}}} g_{{\text{lib}}} \frac{\bar {Y}}{Y_{{\text{lib}}}}\right)^{-1},$$\end{document}(S45)Y¯=(1−xlibYwt+xlibYlib)−1,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \bar {Y} = \left (\frac{1 - x_{{\text{lib}}}}{Y_{{\text{wt}}}}+ \frac{x_{{\text{lib}}}}{Y_{{\text{lib}}}}\right)^{-1},$$\end{document}

where gwt\begin{document}$g_{{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} is the wild-type growth rate, λwt\begin{document}$\lambda _{{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} is the wild-type lag time,(S46)xlib=∑mutsjxj,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle x_{{\text{lib}}} = \sum _{{\text{muts}\,j}}x_{j},$$\end{document}

is the mutant library abundance at the beginning of the bulk competition,(S47)λlib=∑mutsjλjxjxlibgjglibYlibYj\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \lambda _{{\text{lib}}} = \sum _{{\text{muts}\,j}}\lambda _{j} \frac{x_{j}}{x_{{\text{lib}}}}\frac{ g_{j}}{g_{{\text{lib}}}}\frac{Y_{{\text{lib}}}}{Y_{j}}$$\end{document}

is the mutant library lag time,(S48)glib=∑mutsjgjxjxlibYlibYj\begin{document}$$\displaystyle g_{{\mathrm{lib}}} = \sum _{{\mathrm{muts}\,j}}g_{j} \frac{x_{j}}{x_{\mathrm{lib}}}\frac{Y_{\mathrm{lib}}}{Y_{j}}$$\end{document}

is the mutant library growth rate, and(S49)Ylib=[∑mutsjxjxlib1Yj]−1\begin{document}$$\displaystyle Y_{\mathrm{lib}} = \left [\sum _{{\mathrm{muts}\,j}}\frac{x_{j}}{x_{\mathrm{lib}}}\frac{1}{Y_{j}}\right ]^{-1}$$\end{document}

is the mutant library yield. Note that the effective traits in Equations S47–S49 are independent under a rescaling of the mutant library abundance xlib\begin{document}$x_{{\mathrm{lib}}}$\end{document} as long as the relative proportion of the individual lineages xj/xlib\begin{document}$x_{j}/x_{{\mathrm{lib}}}$\end{document} stays constant.

To simplify calculations, we sometimes assume that the mutants have variation in lag time and growth rate, but no variation in biomass yield (Yi=Yj\begin{document}$Y_{i} = Y_{j}$\end{document} for all i\begin{document}$\(i\)$\end{document} and j\begin{document}$\(j\)$\end{document}). Under this assumption, we can rewrite Equations S43 and S44 as(S50)λ¯=(1−xlib)gwtλwt+xlibglibλlib(1−xlib)gwt+xlibglib,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \bar {\lambda } = \frac{(1-x_{{\text{lib}}}) {g_{\text{wt}}}\lambda _{{\text{wt}}} + x_{{\text{lib}}} g_{{\text{lib}}} \lambda _{{\text{lib}}} }{(1 - x_{{\text{lib}}})g_{{\text{wt}}} + x_{{\text{lib}}} g_{{\text{lib}}}},$$\end{document}(S51)τ¯=1(1−xlib)gwt+xlibglib.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \bar {\tau } = \frac{1}{(1 - x_{{\text{lib}}})g_{{\text{wt}}} + x_{{\text{lib}}} g_{{\text{lib}}}}.$$\end{document}

sec.title: S8. Epistasis detection for double mutants using relative fitness per-cycle and per-generation
sec.p: In this section, we discuss the patterns of epistasis observed in relative fitness per-cycle and relative fitness per-generation for the systematic scan of double mutants in our model of population dynamics (Methods). For relative fitness per-cycle, main text Figure 3C shows that epistasis occurs if and only if one of the mutations involves a change in growth rate. This is because the selection on growth rate in the per-cycle statistic depends on the duration of the growth cycle (Manhart et al., 2018)(S52)scyclelogit=gmut(tsat−λmut)−gwt(tsat−λwt),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle {s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}}= {g_{\mathrm{mut}}}({t_{\mathrm{sat}}}- {\lambda_{\mathrm{mut}}}) - {g_{\mathrm{wt}}}({t_{\mathrm{sat}}}- {\lambda_{\mathrm{wt}}}),$$\end{document}

where tsat\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{sat}}}$\end{document} is the saturation time, tsat−λmut\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{sat}}}- {\lambda_{\mathrm{mut}}}$\end{document} is the time of growth for the mutant strain and tsat−λwt\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{sat}}}- {\lambda_{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} is the time of growth for the wild-type strain. At high relative abundance of the mutant, the saturation time tsat\begin{document}${t_{\text{sat}}}$\end{document} depends on all three mutant traits (Equation S38), leading to quadratic mutant trait terms in Equation S52 and non-zero epistasis in main text Equation 17. For example, a double mutant in growth rate (+g,+g\begin{document}$+g, +g$\end{document}) has lower than expected relative fitness per-cycle (negative epistasis in Equation 17) because the second growth rate mutation shortens the growth window tsat−λmut\begin{document}${t_{\text{sat}}}-{\lambda_{\text{mut}}}$\end{document} in Equation S52 (see growth curves in Appendix 1—figure 9; row A). Intuitively, there is no epistasis between lag time and yield because changes to lag time play out early in the growth cycle and changes in yield only change the final time point of growth (see Appendix 1—figure 11). Note that here we have chosen examples where both mutants exit the lag phase before saturation—for deleterious mutations with extremely long lag time, a double mutant (+λ,+λ)\begin{document}$(+\lambda , +\lambda)$\end{document} eventually shows epistasis in relative fitness per-cycle since the wild-type growth advantage is bounded from above due to finite resources.

Using relative fitness per-generation sgen\begin{document}${s_{\text{gen}}}$\end{document}, main text Figure 3D shows that epistasis occurs if and only if one of the mutations involves lag time, a pattern that is distinct from the per-cycle statistic (compare Figure 3C, D). This is because the relative fitness per-generation uses the wild-type LFC as a normalizing time scale (main text Equation 10) and nonlinearities in this time scale with respect to the mutant traits can modify or create new epistasis. For example, epistasis is modified in the per-generation statistic for a double mutant in growth rate and lag time (e.g., (+g,−λ)\begin{document}$(+g,-\lambda)$\end{document}; Appendix 1—figure 9, row D). There is positive epistasis in relative fitness per-cycle, since the shorter lag time leads to a longer mutant growth time which amplifies selection on growth rate (compare Equation S52), but there is even higher positive epistasis in the per-generation statistic, because the double mutant growth is spread over less wild-type generations compared to the single mutant growth. Sometimes, the nonlinearity in the time-scale LFCwt\begin{document}${\text{LFC}}_{\text{wt}}$\end{document} works to remove epistasis. For example, a double-mutant of growth rate (+g,+g)\begin{document}$\((+g,+g)\)$\end{document} (Appendix 1—figure 9, row A) is epistatic in the per-cycle statistic but non-epistatic in the per-generation statistic(S53)sgenlogit=gmut(tsat−λmut)gwt(tsat−λwt)−1,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle {s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\text{gen}}}= \frac{{g_{\text{mut}}}({t_{\text{sat}}}- {\lambda_{\text{mut}}})}{{g_{\text{wt}}}({t_{\text{sat}}}- {\lambda_{\text{wt}}})}- 1,$$\end{document}

where the mutant growth time tsat−λmut\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{sat}}}- {\lambda_{\mathrm{mut}}}$\end{document} and the wild-type tsat−λwt\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{sat}}}- {\lambda_{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} are both reduced but happen to cancel. Finally, the mutant-dependent time-scale LFCwt\begin{document}${\mathrm{LFC}}_{\mathrm{wt}}$\end{document} of the per-generation statistic also introduces new epistasis between lag time and yield (Appendix 1—figure 11), as well as for mutants with two lag time mutations (Appendix 1—figure 11, row C and Appendix 1—figure 12, row D). These mutations have no epistasis in relative fitness per-cycle but the normalization by the wild-type LFC in main text Equation 10 introduces an additional dependence on tsat\begin{document}${t_{\text{sat}}}$\end{document} that renders fitness a quadratic function of lag time.

We repeat the fitness estimates using a 1% mutant relative abundance in the simulated competition experiments (Appendix 1—figure 15A). At this low mutant abundance, Appendix 1—figure 15B shows the epistasis in relative fitness per-cycle scycle\begin{document}${s_{\mathrm{cycle}}}$\end{document} is limited to combinations of mutants that perturb growth rate and lag time. Note that in this low abundance limit, the relative fitness per-generation sgen\begin{document}${s_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document} agrees on the presence and absence of epistasis (Appendix 1—figure 15C), simply because the wild-type LFC is approximately constant across mutants.

sec.title: S9. Analysis of fitness trajectories from the Long-Term Evolution Experiment
sec.p: A previous analysis of the Long-Term Evolution Experiment (LTEE) performed by Wiser et al., 2013 found that evolved populations of Escherichia coli increased in relative fitness over 50,000 generations without converging to a maximum fitness. Here, we re-analyze the same data by directly comparing the relative fitness (under the logit encoding) per-cycle scyclelogit\begin{document}${s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}}$\end{document} and per-generation sgenlogit\begin{document}${s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document} to see if the choice of fitness statistic changes the conclusion. The experimental protocol of the LTEE has been described elsewhere (Lenski et al., 1991; Barrick et al., 2023), but we briefly summarize the main aspects: Starting with a single ancestral strain of E. coli, 12 replicate populations were inoculated in 1988 and are perpetually grown in batch cultures with serial transfers, such that 1% of the population biomass is transferred to fresh growth medium each day. Samples from each replicate population are stored every 500 generations, leading to a record of evolved populations over time (Barrick et al., 2023).

Previous work performed competition experiments between the ancestral population and each evolved population (every 500–2000 generations) by combining them in equal proportions and growing them over a single batch culture growth cycle, with measurements of their initial and final absolute abundances taken by colony counting (Wiser et al., 2013). This data has been prepared in a convenient format by Good et al., 2017 and is available for download here. The total data set lists n = 928 competition experiments. We remove n=6 entries because either the initial or final abundances are missing.

For a few of the 12 populations, the time series is truncated: population Ara+6 has competition measurements up to generation 4000, population Ara-2 has competition measurements up to generation 30,000, and population Ara+2 has competition measurements up to generation 32,000 (Wiser et al., 2013). Note that the evolved population tested in these competitions is not a single genotype, but a sample of many genotypes that were present in that evolving population at that time. From these values of absolute abundance, we compute the log fold-change (LFC) of the evolved and ancestral populations in each competition and then calculate the evolved population’s relative fitness per-cycle (main text Equation 9) and per-generation (main text Equation 10). The original data set has two to four replicate measurements for each evolved sample, corresponding to a repeat of the competition experiment at a different day (Wiser et al., 2013). Initially, we collect all competition experiments into a single data set (n = 928 competitions) and find that relative fitness per-generation and per-cycle differ in the ranking of these competitions (main text Figure 4B, Appendix 1—figure 17A). For example, one competition is ranked 261 positions lower in relative fitness per-generation than per-cycle (where higher rank indicates higher fitness). The scatter occurs because the biomass yield evolves downward over time (Vasi et al., 1994; Grant et al., 2021). We can understand the ranking mismatch from the underlying LFCs in the competition experiment (Appendix 1—figure 17B), that show considerable scatter, with some mutant-wild-type pairs in a positive covariation (compare Appendix 1—figure 17B and main text Figure 1D). The scatter occurs because the biomass yield evolves downward over time (Vasi et al., 1994; Grant et al., 2021), shifting the wild-type LFCs downward in 1:1 competitions with the evolved populations (horizontal trend across time points in Appendix 1—figure 17B).

We can also construct a time series of relative fitness for each population and compare fitness rankings at individual time points. For each of the 12 populations in the LTEE, we define the relative fitness per-generation sgenlogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document} at time t by averaging the value sgenlogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document} across all competition experiments with the frozen sample from time t\begin{document}$\(t\)$\end{document}. Similarly, we define a time series of relative fitness per-cycle scyclelogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}}$\end{document} for each population. In summary, we can pool all time series into a single data set (with the truncation described above) and test how the two statistics rank the 12 populations at any point in the experiment. We find that the mismatch between relative fitness per-cycle and per-generation is consistently low at all time points (main text Figure 4A), with a few exceptions (for example, at generation 4000 the two statistics disagree on the top six populations).

A key result from previous analysis by Wiser et al., 2013 on this data set is that the evolving populations increase indefinitely in relative fitness, rather than leveling off at some maximum fitness value. The empirical analysis by Wiser et al., 2013 tested the long-term trend by fitting the statistic W=1+sgenlogit\begin{document}$W = 1 + {s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document} to a hyperbolic model of the time series:(S54)f(t)=1+att+b,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle f(t) = 1 + \frac{at}{t+b},$$\end{document}

where t\begin{document}$\(t\)$\end{document} is the evolutionary time point at which the evolved population is measured against its ancestor, and f(t)\begin{document}$f(t)$\end{document} is the fitness statistic measured from that competition (here fitted to the measured values of W). The important feature of the hyperbolic model is that it assumes that relative fitness saturates at a maximum fitness over long times (limt→∞f(t)=1+a\begin{document}$\lim _{t\to \infty }f(t) = 1+a$\end{document}). To contrast this model, they also tested a power law(S55)f(t)=(αt+1)β\begin{document}$$\displaystyle f(t) = (\alpha t + 1)^{\beta }$$\end{document}

under which fitness increases without bound over long times (limt→∞f(t)=∞\begin{document}$\lim _{t\to \infty }f(t) = \infty $\end{document}). To repeat this analysis with the fitness statistics scyclelogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}}$\end{document} and sgenlogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document} used in this article, we must adjust the models to account for the fact that W takes 1 as its neutral value (occurring at t=0\begin{document}$\(t =0\)$\end{document} by definition) while scyclelogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}}$\end{document} and sgenlogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document} are zero under neutrality. Thus, we use(S56)f(t)=att+b\begin{document}$$\displaystyle f(t) = \frac{at}{t+b}$$\end{document}
as the hyperbolic model and(S57)f(t)=(αt)β\begin{document}$$\displaystyle f(t) = (\alpha t)^{\beta }$$\end{document}
as the power law model.

As a control against the original analysis of Wiser et al., 2013, we first perform our own fit of the time series of the relative fitness per-generation sgenlogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document} to the hyperbolic (Equation S56) and the power law (Equation S57) models. Wiser et al. compared their two models using the Bayesian Information Criterion but since the models have the same number of parameters this is mathematically equivalent to comparing the values of R2\begin{document}$R^{2}$\end{document}. Appendix 1—figure 16A shows that in our analysis, the power law model has a higher quality of fit (R2=0.701\begin{document}$R^{2} = 0.701$\end{document}) than the hyperbolic model does (R2=0.682\begin{document}$\(R^{2} = 0.682\)$\end{document}) for the fitness statistic sgenlogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document}, consistent with the original result by Wiser et al. for the statistic W=1+sgenlogit\begin{document}$W=1+{s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\text{gen}}}$\end{document}. Since the equations for the hyperbolic model only differ in the constant offset (compare Equations S54 and S56), our fit of sgenlogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document} to Equation S56 is mathematically equivalent to the fit of W to Equation S54. Therefore, our fit should give the exact same results as the original publication (Wiser et al., 2013) in the case of the hyperbolic model (although we could not find the fitted values a,b\begin{document}$\(a,b\)$\end{document} documented in the original publication so we were unable to check them). This is not true for the power law, because the modified power law used by Wiser et al. (Equation S55) includes the offset within the parentheses, rather than as an added constant outside (compare Equation S55 to Equation S57). This means that the fit of W\begin{document}$\(W\)$\end{document} to the power law with an initial value of 1 (Equation S55, fitted values α=0.00515,β=0.0950\begin{document}$\alpha =0.00515, \beta =0.0950$\end{document}; matching Wiser et al., 2013) is different from the fit of sgenlogit\begin{document}${s^{\text{logit}}_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document} to the power law with an initial value of zero (Equation S57, fitted values α=0.000007,β=0.299891\begin{document}$\(\alpha =0.000007, \beta =0.299891\)$\end{document}).

We next perform a new analysis by calculating the relative fitness per-cycle scyclelogit\begin{document}${s^{\text{logit}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}}$\end{document} from the same time series data (12 time series pooled together, one for each line) and fitting this fitness statistic to the same hyperbolic (Equation S56) and power law (Equation S57) models. As shown in Appendix 1—figure 16B, we find that the power law model outperforms the hyperbolic model for the per-cycle fitness, consistent with the model performance for the per-generation fitness. This suggests that Wiser et al.’s original conclusion about fitness increasing without bound (Wiser et al., 2013) is robust to the choice of fitness statistic.

As we previously mentioned, the fitness measurements of all replicate populations are not uniform across time (Appendix 1—figure 16A): there are fewer fitness measurements at late time points (generation 34,000 and higher) because three populations were eventually excluded from the fitness measurements (Wiser et al., 2013). To further corroborate our results, we thus repeat the model fits using a single time series of the evolved fitness, rather than fitting the models to all 12 fitness time series simultaneously. We calculate the average fitness per-generation sgenlogit\begin{document}${s^{\rm logit}_{\mathrm{gen}}}$\end{document} and per-cycle scyclelogit\begin{document}${s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}}$\end{document} in the evolution experiment as the average across all 12 populations at each time point and fit this population-averaged time series to the hyperbolic (Equation S56) and power law (Equation S57) models (Wiser et al. refer to this as a fit to the ‘grand mean’). Appendix 1—figure 16C, D shows that the power law still has a better quality of fit than the hyperbolic model does, and we thus conclude that the increasing fitness trend reported by Wiser et al., 2013 is also robust to the uneven distribution of measurements over time.

We note that the quality of fit R reported in the main text of Wiser et al., 2013 differs from the quality of fit we show on our plots. While both studies performed the fits of the models on all 12 populations simultaneously, Wiser et al., 2013, evaluated the quality of fit by calculating R for the fitted model (blue and pink lines in Appendix 1—figure 16A) against the fitness time series averaged over replicates (gray points in Appendix 1—figure 16C). That is, they fit the model to the data without averaging over population but calculate quality of fit using the population-averaged data. Since we believe this was inconsistent, we have followed a more standard approach of calculating the quality of fit on the same input data used for the fit (i.e., correlating the blue and pink lines in Appendix 1—figure 16A with gray points in the same plot). As a consequence, the correlations between the fitted models and data reported in the original publication (hyperbolic R=0.969\begin{document}$R=0.969$\end{document}, power law R=0.986\begin{document}$R=0.986$\end{document}; see Wiser et al., 2013) are systematically higher than the values we find in our re-analysis (hyperbolic R=0.826\begin{document}$R=0.826$\end{document}, power law: R=0.837\begin{document}$R=0.837$\end{document}; take square root of the values in Appendix 1—figure 16A). Although the long-term fitness dynamics in the case of the LTEE are robust to the choice of fitness statistic, we note that it is possible to construct scenarios of microbial growth trait evolution where relative fitness saturates in one statistic but not in the other (main text Figure 3E–F). For theory work on the long-term trend of fitness in evolving populations and additional models beyond the power law, see Sibani et al., 1998; Park and Krug, 2008; Guo et al., 2019; Guo and Amir, 2022; Boffi et al., 2024.

sec.title: S10. Testing AUC and other fitness potentials using simulated competition experiments
sec.p: In this section, we explain our tests of estimated fitness potentials against true relative fitness in simulated competition experiments. We first focus on the area under the growth curve (AUC), which is defined as(S58)AUC=∫0tevalN(t)dt,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle {\text{AUC}}= \int _{0}^{{t_{\text{eval}}}}N(t) dt,$$\end{document}

where N(t)\begin{document}$\(N(t)\)$\end{document} is a growth curve of absolute abundance (or a proxy such as optical density) and teval\begin{document}${t_{\text{eval}}}$\end{document} is a cutoff time for evaluating the area. Many previous studies (Worthan et al., 2023; Schmitz et al., 2024; Sprouffske et al., 2018; Piccardi et al., 2019; Dos Santos et al., 2022) and growth curve analysis packages (Sprouffske and Wagner, 2016) have used this definition. The idea of AUC is that, unlike estimated fitness potentials that only account for individual traits of a genotype’s growth (e.g., growth rate or lag time; see below), the AUC literally integrates the whole growth dynamics into a single number. For example, both fast growth rate and short lag time are manifested in greater AUC. Note that while one can attempt to use the AUC as an approximate fitness potential (as we investigate here), it is not a measure of absolute fitness (Appendix 1—section S2) since it is insufficient to predict changes in absolute abundance (i.e., the area under the growth curve does not determine the change in absolute abundance from beginning to end).

To compute the AUC for the set of single-gene deletion genotypes in our data set, we first simulate a growth curve for each genotype under the population dynamics model in main text Equation 12a with the traits estimated from the yeast single-gene knockout data (Methods). We use simulated growth curves, with trait values inferred from the measured growth curves, rather than the actual measured growth curves since we are comparing the AUCs to relative fitness also from simulations of competitions; we do not have actual competition data for these genotypes, so it would be an apples-to-oranges comparison if we used AUCs from the actual growth curve data. Furthermore, in empirical growth curves, the AUC is also influenced by technical variation in the initial biomass N0\begin{document}$N_{0}$\end{document} and the initial concentration of resources R0\begin{document}$R_{0}$\end{document}, so using simulations removes these effects.

Appendix 1—figure 20A shows the distribution of saturation times tsat\begin{document}${t_{\text{sat}}}$\end{document} (as defined for the population dynamics model in Methods) numerically calculated for all simulated growth curves of the deletion mutants. We calculate the AUC for each growth curve using Equation S58 with an evaluation time of teval=16\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{eval}}}= 16$\end{document} hr since that includes the stationary phase in the vast majority of our simulated growth curves (Appendix 1—figure 20A). From the mutant’s AUC, we calculate the AUC-based estimator of the mutant’s relative fitness(S59)s^AUC=AUCmut−AUCwt,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \hat {s}_{{\text{AUC}}} = {\text{AUC}}_{{\text{mut}}} - {\text{AUC}}_{\text{wt}},$$\end{document}

where AUCwt\begin{document}${\text{AUC}}_{{\text{wt}}}$\end{document} is the AUC for a simulated growth curve of the wild-type (using the median wild-type traits in our database; see Methods). We then simulate a single growth cycle of the mutant competing against the wild-type (Equation 12a with equal initial abundance of the mutant and wild-type) to calculate the mutant’s ‘true’ (under the model assumptions) relative fitness per-cycle with the logit encoding scyclelogit\begin{document}$s^{{\text{logit}}}_{{\text{cycle}}}$\end{document}. We simulate both the coculture and the monoculture growth dynamics with the same initial biomass N0=0.05\begin{document}$\(N_{0} = 0.05\)$\end{document} OD and resource concentration R0=111\begin{document}$R_{0} = 111$\end{document} mM (Warringer et al., 2003). Repeating this analysis for all mutant genotypes in the data set, we calculate the Spearman rank correlation between the AUC-predicted relative fitness from monoculture s^AUC\begin{document}$\hat {s}_{{\text{AUC}}}$\end{document} and the true relative fitness in competition scyclelogit\begin{document}$s^{{\text{logit}}}_{{\text{cycle}}}$\end{document} (Appendix 1—figure 19, column C).

The success of the AUC depends on the evaluation time teval\begin{document}$t_{\text{eval}}$\end{document}, which sets the time window from which information is captured from the growth curve by the integral (Equation S58). Appendix 1—figure 20B–D shows the correlation between the relative fitness in coculture scyclelogit\begin{document}${s^{{\text{logit}}}_{\mathrm{cycle}}}$\end{document} and the AUC estimator s^AUC\begin{document}$\hat {s}_{{\mathrm{AUC}}}$\end{document} (Equation S59) for three values of teval\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{eval}}}$\end{document}: the mean saturation time of all genotypes in monoculture (teval≈13\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{eval}}}\approx 13$\end{document} hr), a significantly longer value (teval≈24\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{eval}}}\approx 24$\end{document} hr), and an intermediate value (teval=16\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{eval}}}=16$\end{document} hr; used for Appendix 1—figure 19). For short evaluation times (teval≈13\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{eval}}}\approx 13$\end{document} hr), the AUC underestimates the fitness of mutants with long lag but fast growth, which leads to a nonlinear relationship between the AUC estimator and the true relative fitness (compare Appendix 1—figure 20B, C). For long evaluation times (teval=24\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{eval}}}=24$\end{document} hr), there is greater scatter between the AUC predictor and true relative fitness for the highest fitness mutants (compare spread in Appendix 1—figure 20C, D). Intuitively, these mutants have short lag times or fast growth rates and saturate early in monoculture, so their AUC values are effectively set by the biomass yield, which has no predictive value on the competition outcome. In summary, Appendix 1—figure 20B–D shows a trade-off between accurately ranking highly deleterious mutants (which need long teval\begin{document}$t_{\mathrm{eval}}$\end{document}) and ranking highly beneficial mutants (which need short teval\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{eval}}}$\end{document}).

Besides AUC, it is possible to use other features of the monoculture growth curve as approximate fitness potentials. For example, one can use the monoculture growth rates alone as fitness potentials:(S60)s^g=gmutmono−gwtmono,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \hat {s}_{g} = {g^{{\mathrm{mono}}}_{\mathrm{mut}}} - {g^{{\mathrm{mono}}}_{\mathrm{wt}}},$$\end{document}

or the monoculture lag times:(S61)s^lag=λmutmono−λwtmono.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \hat {s}_{{\mathrm{lag}}} = {\lambda^{{\mathrm{mono}}}_{\mathrm{mut}}} - {\lambda}^{{\mathrm{mono}}}_{\mathrm{wt}}.$$\end{document}

Another possible fitness potential is the absolute abundance at saturation, which in our model of population dynamics (Equation 12a) is proportional to the biomass yield:(S62)s^Y=Ymutmono−Ywtmono.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \hat {s}_{Y} = {Y^{{\mathrm{mono}}}_{\mathrm{mut}}} - {Y^{{\mathrm{mono}}}_{\mathrm{wt}}}.$$\end{document}

Finally, one can also use the difference in the monoculture log fold-changes (LFCs):(S63)s^LFC=log⁡(Nmut(tsatmono)Nmut(0))−log⁡(Nwt(tsatmono)Nwt(0)).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \hat {s}_{{\mathrm{LFC}}} = \log \left (\frac{{N_{\mathrm{mut}}}({t^{{\mathrm{mono}}}_{\mathrm{sat}}})}{{N_{\mathrm{mut}}}(0)}\right) -\log \left (\frac{{N_{\mathrm{wt}}}({t^{{\mathrm{mono}}}_{\mathrm{sat}}})}{{N_{\mathrm{wt}}}(0)}\right).$$\end{document}

This looks similar to the definition of relative fitness per-cycle (main text Equation 9) but is distinct because it uses the LFCs in monoculture rather than the true LFCs in coculture (which may be different).

We test each of these fitness potentials against the relative fitness in pairwise competition, using different input data sets of trait variation and the ‘GNU Parallel’ command to speed up the simulation process (Tange, 2018). Appendix 1—figure 19 rows B and C show that growth rate and lag time can act as perfect fitness potentials if that trait is the only trait with variation across mutants. This is because the relative fitness is proportional to differences in each of these traits when they are the only source of variation (see Appendix 1—section S14). Appendix 1—section S14 also shows that differences in biomass yield (Ymut−Ywt\begin{document}${Y_{\mathrm{mut}}}-{Y_{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document}) have no effect on fitness by themselves, which is why the biomass yield of the strains in monoculture is a poor fitness potential to estimate relative fitness. This large but neutral variation in the biomass yield across mutants in our data sets means that the LFC is also a poor fitness potential.

All of these trait-based fitness potentials are outperformed by the AUC, which provides the best approximation of the mutant fitness ranking in coculture under realistic trait variation (Appendix 1—figure 19, row A). More broadly, it is important to treat absolute and relative fitness, as well as fitness potentials, as distinct concepts, serving different purposes (Smith et al., 2024; Gordo et al., 2012). As we show here in simulation (Appendix 1—figure 19), and others have shown in experiments (Concepción-Acevedo et al., 2015; Durão et al., 2021; Worthan et al., 2023; Schmitz et al., 2024), measuring fitness potentials is not enough to demonstrate that a mutant genotype will outcompete the wild-type.

sec.title: S11. Coarse-graining pairwise relative fitness in multi-genotype populations
sec.p: In this section, we point out the specific advantages of the logit-encoding for coarse-graining pairwise relative fitness in bulk competition experiments. While the pairwise relative fitness is defined for any encoding m, the logit encoding endows it with some convenient mathematical properties not shared by other encodings (e.g., the log encoding). The logit encoding of the pairwise relative abundance has the property(S64)logitxij=log⁡xi−log⁡xj,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle {\operatorname{logit}\,}x_{ij}= \log x_{i} - \log x_{j},$$\end{document}

meaning that it is antisymmetric under exchange of the indices i and j (logitxij=−logitxji\begin{document}${\text{logit}}\,x_{ij}= - {\text{logit}}\,x_{ji}$\end{document}) and additive across pairs of indices (logitxij=logitxik+logitxkj\begin{document}${\text{logit}}\,x_{ij}= {\text{logit}}\,x_{ik}+ {\text{logit}}\,x_{kj}$\end{document}). Since the logit-encoded pairwise relative fitness is just the time derivative of the logit function (Equation 21), it carries equivalent properties of antisymmetry and additivity:(S65)sjilogit=−sijlogit,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}_{ji} = - s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}_{ij},$$\end{document}(S66)sijlogit=siklogit+skjlogit.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}_{ij} = s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}_{ik}+ s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}_{kj}.$$\end{document}

We also note that the logit encoding of the pairwise relative abundance has the property:(S67)logit(axiaxi+bxj)=logit(xixi+xj)+log⁡(ab).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle {\operatorname{logit}}\left (\frac{ax_{i}}{ax_{i} + bx_{j}}\right) = {\operatorname{logit}}\left (\frac{x_{i}}{x_{i} + x_{j}}\right) + \log \left (\frac{a}{b}\right).$$\end{document}

Rescaling the relative abundances of either genotype thus does not change the pairwise relative fitness (since it only shifts the logit by a constant, which does not affect its derivative). This means that pairwise relative fitness is an ‘intensive’ property of a genotype, analogous to intensive properties in statistical mechanics (such as temperature) that do not scale with system size. For example, if we split a mutant genotype into two subgroups (e.g., differentiated by a neutral marker), the pairwise relative fitness of each mutant subgroup with respect to the wild-type will be the same as the pairwise relative fitness of the mutant genotype as a whole compared to the wild-type. In contrast, the logit-encoded total relative fitness does not satisfy this property since logit(axi)≠logitxi+a\begin{document}${\text{logit}\,}(ax_{i}) \neq {\text{logit}\,}x_{i} + a$\end{document} .

When the encoding m is the logit function, the pairwise relative fitness per-cycle still satisfies the above properties (antisymmetry and additivity with respect to indices i, j, and invariance under relative abundance rescaling) since those are properties of the underlying logit encoding. This is also apparent from interpreting the per-cycle fitness statistic as an integral of the instantaneous statistic:(S68)sij,cyclem=∫t0tsatsijm(t)dt.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s_{ij, {\text{cycle}}}^{m}= \int _{t_0}^{{t_{\text{sat}}}}s^{m}_{ij}(t)\, dt.$$\end{document}

sec.title: S12. The relative fitness between coarse-grained groups of genotypes
sec.p: In this section, we generalize the concept of pairwise relative fitness to pairs of genotype groups rather than pairs of individual genotypes. In a multi-genotype population with subsets of genotypes A\begin{document}$\mathcal{A}$\end{document} and B\begin{document}$\mathcal{B}$\end{document}, define(S69)xAB(t)=∑i∈Axi(t)∑i∈A∪Bxi(t)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle x_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{B}}(t) = \frac{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} x_i(t)}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{A} \cup \mathcal{B}} x_i(t)}$$\end{document}

as the relative abundance of A\begin{document}$\mathcal{A}$\end{document} genotypes compared to B\begin{document}$\mathcal{B}$\end{document} genotypes at time t, where A∪B\begin{document}$A \cup B$\end{document} is the union of the two index sets. Analogous with main text Equation 21, we define the fitness of group A\begin{document}${\mathcal{A}}$\end{document} relative to group B\begin{document}$\mathcal{B}$\end{document} as(S70)sABm=ddtm(xAB(t))\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{B}}^m = \frac{d}{dt} m(x_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{B}}(t))$$\end{document}

for an encoding m. Under the logit encoding, it turns out that the fitness between these two groups can be conveniently expressed as a weighted average of the pairwise fitness between the member genotypes in each group:(S71)sABlogit=1∑i∈Axi1∑j∈Bxj⋅∑i∈A∑j∈Bxixjsijlogit.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{B}}^{\text{logit}} = \frac{1}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} x_i} \frac{1}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}} x_j} \cdot \sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}} x_i x_j s_{ij}^{\text{logit}}.$$\end{document}

To prove Equation S71, we first note that(S72)xAB1−xAB=∑i∈Axi∑j∈Bxj.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{x_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{B}}}{1 - x_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{B}}} = \frac{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} x_i}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}} x_j}.$$\end{document}

Thus, we can rewrite the logit-encoded relative pairwise fitness between A\begin{document}${\mathcal{A}}$\end{document} and B\begin{document}${\mathcal{B}}$\end{document} as(S73)sABlogit=ddtlogitxAB=ddtlog⁡(∑i∈Axi∑j∈Bxj)=ddtlog⁡(∑i∈Axi)−ddtlog⁡(∑j∈Bxj),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl}s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}_{{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{B}}}&=&\frac{d}{dt}{\operatorname{logit}}\,x_{{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{B}}}\\&=&\frac{d}{dt}\log\left(\frac{\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{A}}}x_i}{\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{B}}}x_j}\right)\\&=&\frac{d}{dt}\log\Bigg(\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{A}}}x_i\Bigg)-\frac{d}{dt}\log\Bigg(\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{B}}}x_j\Bigg),\end{array}$$\end{document}

where we have invoked Equation S72 on the second line. We can expand each term on the right-hand side of Equation S73 as(S74)ddtlog⁡∑i∈Axi=1∑i∈Axi∑i∈Adxidt,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{d}{dt}\log \sum _{i\in {\mathcal{A}}}x_{i}= \frac{1}{\sum _{i\in {\mathcal{A}}}x_{i}}\sum _{i\in {\mathcal{A}}}\frac{dx_{i}}{dt},$$\end{document}

and then insert Equation S74 into Equation S73 to obtain(S75)sABlogit=1∑i∈Axi1∑j∈Bxj⋅[∑j∈Bxj∑i∈Adxidt−∑i∈Axi∑j∈Bdxjdt],\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{B}}^{\text{logit}} = \frac{1}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} x_i} \frac{1}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}} x_j} \cdot \left[ \sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}} x_j \sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} \frac{dx_i}{dt} - \sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} x_i \sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}} \frac{dx_j}{dt} \right],$$\end{document}

where we have collected the normalization factors (sums over relative abundances in A\begin{document}${\mathcal{A}}$\end{document} and B\begin{document}${\mathcal{B}}$\end{document}) as a single pre-factor. We then rewrite each product of sums in Equation S75 as(S76)∑j∈Bxj∑i∈Adxidt=∑j∈B∑i∈Axjxiddtlog⁡xi\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}} x_j \sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} \frac{dx_i}{dt} = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} x_j x_i \frac{d}{dt} \log x_i$$\end{document}

to finally obtain(S77)sABlogit=1∑i∈Axi1∑j∈Bxj⋅[∑j∈B∑i∈Axjxi(ddtlog⁡xi−ddtlog⁡xj)].\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl}s^{{\text{logit}}}_{{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{B}}}&=&\frac{1}{\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{A}}}x_i}\frac{1}{\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{B}}}x_j}\\&&\cdot\Bigg[\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{B}}}\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{A}}}x_jx_i\bigg(\frac{d}{dt}\log x_i-\frac{d}{dt}\log x_j\bigg)\Bigg].\end{array}$$\end{document}

Identifying the term in the inner parentheses as the pairwise selection coefficient sijlogit\begin{document}$\(s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}_{ij}\)$\end{document} (main text Equation 21) then results in Equation S71.

Equation S71 establishes that the relative fitness between a pair of genotype groups is a weighted sum of relative fitnesses between individual pairs of genotypes in those groups, but this holds for relative fitness defined at an instant in time (since it is based on derivatives). For relative fitness defined over a finite time interval (e.g., a growth cycle in batch culture), an analogous but approximate result holds. We first write the relative fitness over a growth cycle time interval as an integral over the instantaneous relative fitness (inserting Equation S71 into Equation S68):(S78)sAB,cyclelogit=∫0tsat1∑i∈Axi(t)1∑j∈Bxj(t)⋅∑i∈A∑j∈Bxi(t)xj(t)sijlogit(t)dt,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \begin{array}{ll} s_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{B},\text{cycle}}^{\text{logit}} & = \int_0^{t_{\text{sat}}} \frac{1}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} x_i(t)} \frac{1}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}} x_j(t)} \\ & \cdot \sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}} x_i(t) x_j(t) s_{ij}^{\text{logit}}(t) dt, \end{array}$$\end{document}

where tsat\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{sat}}}$\end{document} is the end time of the growth cycle (Methods, Appendix 1—section S7). The integral in Equation S78 is difficult to calculate as the relative abundance trajectories xi(t),xj(t)\begin{document}$x_{i}(t),x_{j}(t)$\end{document} depend on the relative fitness of the genotypes sijlogit(t)\begin{document}$s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}_{ij}(t)$\end{document} in a non-trivial way. Instead, we make the approximation that the relative abundances do not change significantly over time of the growth cycle (xi(t)≈xi(0)\begin{document}$x_{i}(t) \approx x_{i}(0)$\end{document}) and can thus pass the integral through the sums in Equation S78 to show that the per-cycle relative fitness between a pair of genotype groups is approximately also a weighted sum of per-cycle relative fitnesses:(S79)sAB,cyclelogit≈1∑i∈Axi(0)1∑j∈Bxj(0)⋅∑i∈A∑j∈Bxi(0)xj(0)sij,cyclelogit.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \begin{array}{ll} s_{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{B},\text{cycle}}^{\text{logit}} & \approx \frac{1}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} x_i(0)} \frac{1}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}} x_j(0)}\\ & \cdot \sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}} x_i(0) x_j(0) s_{ij,\text{cycle}}^{\text{logit}}. \end{array}$$\end{document}

Conceptually, assuming the relative abundances are approximately constant over the growth cycle is equivalent to assuming selection is weak; one can also show this mathematically by expressing the relative abundances xi(t)\begin{document}$x_{i}(t)$\end{document} in terms of the pairwise relative fitnesses sijlogit\begin{document}$\(s_{ij}^{{\operatorname{logit}}}\)$\end{document} in Equation S78 and keeping only terms to leading order in sijlogit\begin{document}$s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}_{ij}$\end{document}.
