We finally note that the total relative fitness (instantaneous Equation 19 and per-cycle Equation 22 in the main text) is a special case of the relative fitness between groups (Equations S71 and S79) where A\begin{document}${\mathcal{A}}$\end{document} is the single genotype i and B\begin{document}$\mathcal{B}$\end{document} is all other genotypes besides i:(S80)σilogit=11−xi⋅∑j≠ixjsijlogit,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \sigma _{i}^{{\operatorname{logit}}} = \frac{1}{1 - x_{i}}\cdot \sum _{j\neq i}x_{j} s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}_{ij},$$\end{document}(S81)σi,cyclelogit≈11−xi(0)⋅∑j≠ixj(0)sij,cyclelogit.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \sigma _{i, {\text{cycle}}}^{{\text{logit}}} \approx \frac{1}{1- x_{i}(0)}\cdot \sum _{j\neq i}x_{j}(0) s^{{\text{logit}}}_{ij,{\text{cycle}}}.$$\end{document}

sec.title: S13. Fitness error from the frame of reference in bulk competition experiments
sec.p: Here, we calculate the error that arises from measuring the total relative fitness of each mutant in a bulk competition experiment of a mutant library, rather than the pairwise relative fitness between each mutant and the wild-type. We call this difference the error from the frame of reference, the frame of reference being either the whole population in total fitness or the wild-type in pairwise fitness. Note that this is an error between two different fitness quantifications of the same bulk competition experiment; Appendix 1—section S15 addresses the error (arising from higher-order interactions) between fitness quantifications in bulk versus pairwise competition experiments. Here, we only consider relative fitness under the logit encoding and measured per growth cycle, so we drop these labels to simplify notation.

Consider a bulk competition experiment of a wild-type and a library of large number of mutants over a single batch growth cycle of time tsat\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{sat}}}$\end{document} (Methods). The total relative fitness of mutant i is (main text Equation 22)(S82)σi=logitxi(tsat)−logitxi(0),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \sigma _{i}= {\operatorname{logit}}\, x_{i}({t_{\text{sat}}}) - {\operatorname{logit}}\, x_{i} (0),$$\end{document}

while its pairwise relative fitness compared to the wild-type is (main text Equation 23)(S83)si,wt=logitxi,wt(tsat)−logitxi,wt(0).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s_{i,{\text{wt}}}= {\text{logit}}\, x_{i,{\text{wt}}}({t_{\text{sat}}}) - {\text{logit}}\, x_{i,{\text{wt}}}(0).$$\end{document}

Using the coarse-graining rules from Appendix 1—section S12 (namely Equations S79 and S81), we can express the total relative fitness of mutant i as a weighted sum of the pairwise relative fitnesses between the mutant and the wild-type and between the mutant and the rest of the mutant library:(S84)σi≈1xwt+xlib∖i(xwtsi,wt+xlib∖isi, lib∖i),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \sigma _{i}\approx \frac{1}{x_{{\text{wt}}} + x_{{\text{lib}\backslash i}}}\Big (x_{{\text{wt}}} s_{i,{\text{wt}}}+ x_{{\text{lib}\backslash i}} s_{i,{\text{ lib}\backslash i}}\Big),$$\end{document}

where the notation lib∖i\begin{document}$\text{lib}\backslash i$\end{document} refers to the mutant library excluding the mutant i. The approximation here is due to our assumption in Equation S79 that selection is weak enough that the relative abundances of genotypes do not change too much over the growth cycle. Since we can rewrite the pairwise relative fitness between mutant i\begin{document}$\(i\)$\end{document} and the rest of the library as a difference between i and the wild-type and the rest of the library and the wild-type (using Equation S66)(S85)si,lib∖i=si,wt−slib∖i,wt,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s_{i,{\text{lib}\backslash i}}= s_{i,{\text{wt}}}- s_{{\text{lib}\backslash i},{\text{wt}}},$$\end{document}

we insert this into Equation S84 to obtain(S86)σi≈si,wt−xlib∖ixwt+xlib∖islib∖i,wt.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \sigma _{i}\approx s_{i,{\text{wt}}}- \frac{x_{{\text{lib}\backslash i}}}{x_{{\text{wt}}} + x_{{\text{lib}\backslash i}}}s_{{\text{lib}\backslash i},{\text{wt}}}.$$\end{document}

The difference between the total and pairwise relative fitness is therefore(S87)σi−si,wt≈−xlib∖ixwt+xlib∖islib∖i,wt.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \sigma _{i}- s_{i,{\text{wt}}}\approx - \frac{x_{{\text{lib}\backslash i}}}{x_{{\text{wt}}} + x_{{\text{lib}\backslash i}}}s_{{\text{lib}\backslash i},{\text{wt}}}.$$\end{document}

Since mutant libraries in these experiments typically contain hundreds or thousands of mutants, the contribution of a single mutant i is small and thus we can assume that the properties of the mutant library excluding mutant i (lib∖i\begin{document}${\text{lib}\backslash i}$\end{document}) are approximately the same as the library as a whole (so that xlib∖i≈xlib\begin{document}$x_{{\text{lib}\backslash i}} \approx x_{{\text{lib}}}$\end{document}, slib∖i,wt≈slib,wt\begin{document}$s_{{\text{lib}\backslash i},{\text{wt}}}\approx s_{{\text{lib}},{\text{wt}}}$\end{document}). This allows us to further simplify the error as(S88)σi−si,wt≈−xlibslib,wt.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \sigma _{i}- s_{i,{\text{wt}}}\approx - x_{{\text{lib}}} s_{{\text{lib}},{\text{wt}}}.$$\end{document}

Equation S88 shows why this offset between the total and pairwise relative fitnesses is approximately independent of the focal mutant i (hence the constant shift for all mutant points in main text Figure 5C). The sign of the error from the frame of reference depends on the mean fitness of the mutant library: a mutant library that is overall deleterious relative to the wild-type (slib,wt<0\begin{document}$s_{{\text{lib}},{\text{wt}}} \lt 0$\end{document}) causes the total relative fitness for a mutant σi\begin{document}$\sigma _{i}$\end{document} to overestimate the mutant’s pairwise relative fitness si,wt\begin{document}$s_{i,{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document}. Intuitively, this is because the total relative fitness is comparing the mutant to a mixed population of wild-type and other mutants, which are on average worse competitors than the wild-type, which thus makes the mutant appear to be better than if it is just compared to the wild-type alone (compare top and bottom panel in main text Figure 5B). Equation S88 also shows that the error from the frame of reference can be reduced if the mutant library is neutral relative to the wild-type (slib,wt=0\begin{document}$s_{{\text{lib}},{\text{wt}}}= 0$\end{document}) or the mutant library has small relative abundance in the culture biomass (xlib≪1\begin{document}$x_{{\text{lib}}} \ll 1$\end{document}). In bulk competition experiments with barcoded mutant libraries, these assumptions are often not met since the mutant libraries tend to be overall deleterious (as in our simulated bulk competition for the yeast single-gene knockouts, see Appendix 1—figure 6) and are inoculated at a high relative abundance (Levy et al., 2015; Pierce et al., 2021; Wetmore et al., 2015; Price et al., 2018; Morin et al., 2018). Since this makes the error in Equation S88 significant, we instead recommend including barcoded wild-type strains as references in the bulk competition, so that pairwise fitness can be quantified relative to that (Equation S83) rather than using the total relative fitness. By using a mix of barcoded wild-type cells and non-barcoded wild-type cells, it is further possible to optimize this protocol and save on sequencing investment (Schmidlin et al., 2024).

Finally, we want to point out a difference between the best practice we recommend here (Discussion) and a widespread practice in estimating fitness estimates in bulk competition experiments. In practice, transposon-seq experiments that grow the mutant library by itself start with an estimate of total relative fitness and then subtract the median total relative fitness of the knockouts (Wetmore et al., 2015; Price et al., 2018; Martinson et al., 2023; Morin et al., 2018) or a mean total relative fitness (Levy et al., 2015; Nguyen Ba et al., 2019; Johnson et al., 2019). However, these corrections are not explicitly founded in the choice of a reference group (like a set of neutral genotypes or a wild-type), making the correction appear ad hoc (Wetmore et al., 2015; Martinson et al., 2023; Morin et al., 2018), or the reference is a strain that is not part of the culture, like in the fitness estimates for barcoded lineages that are evaluated against the initial ancestor without that ancestor actually being present (Levy et al., 2015; Nguyen Ba et al., 2019; Johnson et al., 2019). To make things more confusing, even those studies that do include a wild-type then describe their method as an estimate of total relative fitness of the mutant under the log encoding, subtracted by the total relative fitness of the wild-type under the log encoding (Couce et al., 2024; Bakerlee et al., 2021; Schmidlin et al., 2024). The result is a pairwise relative fitness under the logit encoding (Equation 25), but presenting it this way obscures that choice of encoding and the relationship to the classic, logit-based selection coefficient used in pairwise competition experiments (Equation 7). We hope that our framework can provide more clarity: The choice of the reference group happens at the level of relative abundance, by calculating a pairwise relative abundance (Equation 20 or Equation S69), and this removes the need for any correction on the fitness values themselves.

sec.title: S14. Pairwise relative fitness using an explicit model of population dynamics
sec.p: In the model of population dynamics (main text Methods, Equation 12a), we can calculate the pairwise relative fitness of genotypes based on the approximation of the saturation time (Appendix 1—section S7; Manhart et al., 2018; Manhart and Shakhnovich, 2018). The pairwise relative fitness of genotype i\begin{document}$\(i\)$\end{document} relative to genotype j (per-cycle and under the logit encoding) is(S89a)sij,cyclelogit≈sij,lag+sij,growth+sij,coupling,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{{\operatorname{logit}}}_{ij,{\text{cycle}}}\approx s_{ij,{\text{lag}}}+ s_{ij,{\text{growth}}}+ s_{ij,{\text{coupling}}},$$\end{document}

where(S89b)sij,lag=−τ¯τiτjΔλij,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s_{ij,{\text{lag}}}= -\frac{\bar {\tau }}{\tau _{i}\tau _{j}}\Delta \lambda _{ij},$$\end{document}(S89c)sij,growth=−τ¯τiτjΔτijLFC,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s_{ij,{\text{growth}}}= -\frac{\bar {\tau }}{\tau _{i}\tau _{j}}\Delta \tau _{ij}{\text{LFC}},$$\end{document}(S89d)sij,coupling=−τ¯Y¯τiτj×∑kxkτkYk(ΔτikΔλkj−ΔλikΔτkj).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s_{{ij},{\text{coupling}}}=-\frac{\bar{\tau}\bar{Y}}{\tau_i\tau_j}\times\sum_k\frac{x_k}{\tau_kY_k}\left(\Delta\tau_{ik}\Delta\lambda_{kj}-\Delta\lambda_{ik}\Delta\tau_{kj}\right).$$\end{document}

The e\begin{document}$\(e\)$\end{document}-fold growth time for genotype j is τj=1/gj\begin{document}$\tau _{j} = 1/g_{j}$\end{document}, and the terms Δλij=λi−λj\begin{document}$\(\Delta \lambda _{ij}= \lambda _{i} - \lambda _{j}\)$\end{document} and Δτij=τi−τj\begin{document}$\Delta \tau _{ij}= \tau _{i} - \tau _{j}$\end{document} are the differences between the two genotypes' lag times and growth times. Since the terms in Equation S89d depend on the covariation between growth and lag, we interpret these terms as couplings between the growth and lag phases; they are zero if only two genotypes are present.

sec.title: S15. Fitness error from higher-order interactions between pairwise and bulk competition experiments
sec.p: In this section, we calculate the error in relative fitness of a mutant arising from higher-order interactions in bulk competition experiments with large mutant libraries, compared to the ‘true’ relative fitness in pairwise competitions between just the focal mutant and wild-type alone. Here, we only consider relative fitness under the logit encoding and measured per growth cycle, so we drop these labels to simplify notation. Let the pairwise relative fitness of mutant i\begin{document}$\(i\)$\end{document} compared to the wild-type (main text Equation 23) be(S90)si,wtpair=logitxi,wtpair(tsatpair)−logitxi,wt(0)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{{\text{pair}}}_{i,{\text{wt}}}= {\operatorname{logit}}\, x^{{\text{pair}}}_{i,{\text{wt}}}({t^{{\text{pair}}}_{\text{sat}}}) - {\operatorname{logit}}\, x_{i,{\text{wt}}}(0)$$\end{document}

in the pairwise competition with the wild-type alone, and(S91)si,wtbulk=logitxi,wtbulk(tsatbulk)−logitxi,wt(0)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{{\text{bulk}}}_{i,{\text{wt}}}= {\operatorname{logit}}\, x^{{\text{bulk}}}_{i,{\text{wt}}}({t^{{\text{bulk}}}_{\text{sat}}}) - {\operatorname{logit}}\, x_{i,{\text{wt}}}(0)$$\end{document}

in the bulk competition with all other mutants in the library. The superscripts pair and bulk indicate that the dynamics of xi,wt(t)\begin{document}$x_{i,{\mathrm{wt}}}(t)$\end{document} and the saturation time tsat\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{sat}}}$\end{document} may be different in the two competitions. The difference between these two measurements of relative fitness is(S92)Δsi,wt=si,wtbulk−si,wtpair=si,wtpair(si,wtbulksi,wtpair−1).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl}\Delta s_{i,{\text{wt}}}&=&s^{{\text{bulk}}}_{i,{\text{wt}}}-s^{{\text{pair}}}_{i,{\text{wt}}}\\&=&s^{{\text{pair}}}_{i,{\text{wt}}}\left(\frac{s^{{\text{bulk}}}_{i,{\text{wt}}}}{s^{{\text{pair}}}_{i,{\text{wt}}}}-1\right).\end{array}$$\end{document}

Since the difference between the bulk and pairwise competitions is the presence of the other mutants in the library, we interpret this difference as the fitness error from higher-order interactions among the mutants.

We now calculate how this error depends on the underlying growth traits of the genotypes using the population dynamics model (main text Methods, Equation 12a) and the explicit expression for relative fitness from Appendix 1—section S14. Based on the approximate pairwise relative fitness in this model (Equations S89a–S89d), the relative fitness in the pairwise competition is the sum of two terms(S93)si,wtpair=si,wt,lagpair+si,wt,growthpair,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{{\text{pair}}}_{i,{\text{wt}}}= s^{{\text{pair}}}_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{lag}}}+ s^{{\text{pair}}}_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{growth}}},$$\end{document}

while the relative fitness in the bulk competition is the sum of three terms(S94)sibulk=si,lagbulk+si,growthbulk+si,couplingbulk,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{{\text{bulk}}}_{i}= s^{{\text{bulk}}}_{i,{\text{lag}}}+ s^{{\text{bulk}}}_{i,{\text{growth}}}+ s^{{\text{bulk}}}_{i,{\text{coupling}}},$$\end{document}

where the third term represents the coupling between growth and lag phases present only in populations with more than two genotypes (Equation S89d).We define the higher-order effects on the selection for lag time as(S95)Δsi,wt,lag=si,wt,lagbulk−si,wt,lagpair.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Delta s_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{lag}}}= s^{{\text{bulk}}}_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{lag}}}- s^{{\text{pair}}}_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{lag}}}.$$\end{document}

Using Equation S89b, we can express this in terms of the underlying traits as(S96)Δsi,wt,lag=si,wt,lagpair⋅Δτ¯iτ¯pair,i\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Delta s_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{lag}}}= s^{{\text{pair}}}_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{lag}}}\cdot \frac{\Delta {\bar{\tau}}_{i}}{{\bar{\tau}}^{{\text{pair}},i}}$$\end{document}

where Δτ¯i=τ¯bulk−τ¯pair,i\begin{document}$\Delta {\bar{\tau}}_{i} = {\bar{\tau}}^{{\text{bulk}}} - {\bar{\tau}}^{{\text{pair}},i}$\end{document} is the difference in effective e-fold growth times (Equation S40) in the bulk competition and in the pairwise competition of mutant i and the wild-type.

We similarly define the higher-order effects in the selection on growth rate as(S97)Δsi,wt,growth=si,wt,growthbulk−si,wt,growthpair,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Delta s_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{growth}}}= s^{{\text{bulk}}}_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{growth}}}- s^{{\text{pair}}}_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{growth}}},$$\end{document}

and calculate si,wt,growthbulk\begin{document}$s^{{\text{bulk}}}_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{growth}}}$\end{document} and si,wt,growthpair\begin{document}$s^{{\text{pair}}}_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{growth}}}$\end{document} from Equation S89c to get the expression(S98)Δsi,wt,growth=−Δτi,wtτwtτi(τ¯bulkLFCbulk−τ¯pair,iLFCpair,i),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Delta s_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{growth}}}=-\frac{\Delta\tau_{i,{\text{wt}}}}{\tau_{{\text{wt}}}\tau_i}\left({\bar{\tau}}^{{\text{bulk}}}{\text{LFC}}^{{\text{bulk}}}-{\bar{\tau}}^{{\text{pair}},i}{\text{LFC}}^{{\text{pair}},i}\right),$$\end{document}

where LFCbulk\begin{document}${\text{LFC}}^{{\text{bulk}}}$\end{document} is the log fold-change (Equation S42) of the total biomass in the bulk competition and LFCpair,i\begin{document}${\text{LFC}}^{{\text{pair}},i}$\end{document} is the log fold-change of the total biomass in the pairwise competition between mutant i\begin{document}$\(i\)$\end{document} and the wild-type. We note that total biomass growth in the bulk competition LFCbulk\begin{document}${\text{LFC}}^{{\text{bulk}}}$\end{document} depends on the mutant library through the effective biomass yield (Equation S41), but this dependence is weak because the yield enters only logarithmically into Equation S42. We thus assume that the bulk and pairwise competition have equal biomass growth (LFCbulk≈LFCpair,i\begin{document}${\text{LFC}}^{{\text{bulk}}} \approx {\text{LFC}}^{{\text{pair}},i}$\end{document}) for all mutants i\begin{document}$\(i\)$\end{document} such that the higher-order effect on the growth rate selection (Equation S98) is proportional to the increase in the mean doubling time(S99)Δsi,wt,growth≈si,wt,growthpairΔτ¯iτ¯pair,i.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Delta s_{i,\text{wt},\text{growth}} \approx s_{i,\text{wt},\text{growth}}^{\text{pair}} \frac{\Delta \bar{\tau}_i}{\bar{\tau}_{\text{pair},i}} .$$\end{document}

Since this has the same form as the higher-order effect on lag time selection in Equation S96, we can combine Equations S99 and S96 into(S100)Δsi,wt,lag+Δsi,wt,growth≈si,wtpairΔτ¯iτ¯pair,i.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Delta s_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{lag}}}+ \Delta s_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{growth}}}\approx s^{{\text{pair}}}_{i,{\text{wt}}}\frac{\Delta {\bar{\tau}}_{i}}{{\bar{\tau}}^{{\text{pair}},i}}.$$\end{document}

Because the effective growth time in the pairwise competition τ¯pair,i\begin{document}${\bar{\tau}}^{{\mathrm{pair}},i}$\end{document} is approximately just the effective growth time of the wild-type alone τwt\begin{document}$\tau _{{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} (assuming the mutant is competed against it at low initial relative abundance), this means that(S101)Δsi,wt,lag+Δsi,wt,growthsi,wtpair≈(τ¯bulkτwt−1).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{\Delta s_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{lag}}}+ \Delta s_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{growth}}}}{s^{{\text{pair}}}_{i,{\text{wt}}}}\approx \left (\frac{{\bar{\tau}}^{{\text{bulk}}}}{\tau _{{\text{wt}}}}- 1\right).$$\end{document}

That is, the relative error of lag and growth selection from higher-order interactions is approximately independent of the individual mutant, but rather depends on properties of the wild-type (τwt\begin{document}$\tau _{{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document}) and the whole mutant library (through τ¯bulk\begin{document}${\bar{\tau}}^{{\text{bulk}}}$\end{document}). This is why we observe an approximately constant slope across all mutants in Appendix 1—figure 22 (dark orange points) when comparing the error against the pairwise relative fitness. The slight deviation from the constant slope is due to our approximation that the LFCs are the same between the bulk and pairwise competitions; this is a good approximation for the yeast deletion library but not exactly true, and hence causes a slightly different scaling between the growth Δsgrowth\begin{document}$\Delta s_{{\text{growth}}}$\end{document} and lag Δslag\begin{document}$\Delta s_{{\text{lag}}}$\end{document} error terms compared to Equation S101.

Finally, we note that the growth-lag coupling terms si,wt,couplingbulk\begin{document}$s^{{\text{bulk}}}_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{coupling}}}$\end{document} do not have a simple scaling with pairwise relative fitness since they depend quadratically on trait differences; this is shown as the bright orange points in Appendix 1—figure 22. In the main text, we therefore refer to Δsi,wt,lag+Δsi,wt,growth\begin{document}$\Delta s_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{lag}}}+ \Delta s_{i,{\text{wt}},{\text{growth}}}$\end{document} as the fitness-dependent error and the si,wt,couplingbulk\begin{document}$s^{{\mathrm{bulk}}}_{i,{\mathrm{wt}},{\mathrm{coupling}}}$\end{document} as the fitness-independent error from higher-order interactions.

sec.title: S16. Choosing the mutant library abundance in bulk competition experiments
sec.p: Appendix 1—section S15 showed that measuring relative fitness of a mutant in a bulk competition (with a library of other mutants also present) entails an error due to higher-order interactions among the mutants, compared to measuring relative fitness in a pairwise competition consisting of just the mutant and wild-type. Here, we show how this error depends on the relative abundance of the mutant library in the bulk competition, so that we can estimate the range of library abundances that keep the error below a desired threshold.

sec.title: Calculating the relative error on fitness
sec.p: Let the absolute error in relative fitness from higher-order interactions for a mutant i be Δsi,wt\begin{document}$\Delta s_{i,{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} (Equation S92). Let the relative fitness of this mutant in a pairwise competition be si,wtpair\begin{document}$s^{{\text{pair}}}_{i,{\text{wt}}}$\end{document} (Equation S90). Since the error Δsi,wt\begin{document}$\Delta s_{i,{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} depends on the relative abundance xlib\begin{document}$x_{{\mathrm{lib}}}$\end{document} of the whole mutant library, our goal is to determine what range of xlib\begin{document}$x_{{\text{lib}}}$\end{document} keeps the error in relative fitness (compared to the ‘true’ relative fitness in the pairwise competition) below a chosen threshold ϵ\begin{document}$\epsilon$\end{document}:(S102)|Δsi,wtsi,wtpair|<ϵ.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left |\frac{\Delta s_{i,{\text{wt}}}}{s^{{\text{pair}}}_{i,{\text{wt}}}}\right | \lt {\epsilon}.$$\end{document}

In Appendix 1—section S15 we calculated the dependence of Δsi,wt\begin{document}$\Delta s_{i,{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} on the underlying growth traits. However, since here we are mainly concerned with the dependence on the library abundance xlib\begin{document}$x_{{\mathrm{lib}}}$\end{document}, we present an alternative calculation that better captures that dependence.

We start by pointing out that we can express the relative fitness in pairwise (Equation S90) and bulk competitions (Equation S91) in terms of the saturation times for these competitions, using the explicit solution to the population dynamics model in main text Equation 15:(S103)si,wtpair=gi(tsatpair,i−λi)−gwt(tsatpair,i−λwt),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{{\mathrm{pair}}}_{i,{\mathrm{wt}}} = g_{i}({t^{{\mathrm{pair}},i}_{\mathrm{sat}}}- \lambda _{i}) - {g_{\mathrm{wt}}}({t^{{\mathrm{pair}},i}_{\mathrm{sat}}}- \lambda _{{\mathrm{wt}}}),$$\end{document}(S104)si,wtbulk=gi(tsatbulk−λi)−gwt(tsatbulk−λwt).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{{\text{bulk}}}_{i,{\text{wt}}} = g_{i}({t^{{\text{bulk}}}_{\text{sat}}} - \lambda _{i}) - {g_{\text{wt}}}({t^{{\text{bulk}}}_{\text{sat}}} - \lambda _{{\text{wt}}}).$$\end{document}

We can thus express the error from higher-order interactions (Equation S92) as(S105)Δsi,wt=Δgi,wt(tsatbulk−tsatpair,i),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Delta s_{i,{\text{wt}}}= \Delta g_{i,{\text{wt}}}({t^{{\text{bulk}}}_{\text{sat}}} - {t_{\text{sat}}}^{{\text{pair}},i}),$$\end{document}

where Δgi,wt=gi−gwt\begin{document}$\Delta g_{i,{\mathrm{wt}}}= g_{i} - {g_{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document}. Equation S105 shows that the mutant library affects the fitness of individual mutants siwtbulk\begin{document}$s^{{\text{bulk}}}_{i{\text{wt}}}$\end{document} by changing the saturation time. Mathematically, this is equivalent to the results of Appendix 1—section S15, which showed how the difference in effective e-fold growth times τ¯\begin{document}${\bar{\tau}}$\end{document} between bulk and pairwise competitions primarily mediated the higher-order effects, but expressed in terms of the saturation time tsat\begin{document}${t_{\text{sat}}}$\end{document} (which is not identical to τ¯\begin{document}${\bar{\tau}}$\end{document} but related through Equation S38). The error in Equation S105 is also proportional to the growth rate advantage of the mutant compared to the wild-type. In particular, mutant genotypes that only differ in lag time are not affected by the mutant library since their advantage is accrued once at the beginning of the growth cycle and therefore does not scale with the total time of competition.

According to Equation S38, the saturation time tsat\begin{document}${t_{\mathrm{sat}}}$\end{document} depends on the effective lag time λ¯\begin{document}$\bar {\lambda }$\end{document} (Equation S39), effective e-fold growth time τ¯\begin{document}${\bar{\tau}}$\end{document} (Equation S40), and the log fold-change LFC (Equation S42) for the competition. To simplify the calculation, we introduce a few assumptions. We assume all mutants have the same yields as the wild-type (Yi=Ywt\begin{document}$Y_{i}={Y_{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document}) such that the LFCs in the bulk and pairwise competitions are identical (LFCbulk=LFCpair\begin{document}${\mathrm{LFC}}^{{\mathrm{bulk}}} = {\mathrm{LFC}}^{{\mathrm{pair}}}$\end{document}). We also assume that the relative abundance of the mutant in the pairwise competition is small enough that the saturation time in that case is set entirely by the wild-type traits:(S106)tsatpair,i≈λwt+τwtLFC.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle {t^{{\text{pair}},i}_{\text{sat}}}\approx \lambda _{{\text{wt}}} + \tau _{{\text{wt}}}{\text{LFC}}.$$\end{document}

Note that this means that the difference in saturation times is independent of the specific mutant i; the only dependence of the mutant i on the overall error from higher-order interactions is through the difference in growth rates in Equation S105.

We can thus write the fitness error as(S107)Δsi,wt≈Δgi,wt[(λ¯bulk−λwt)+(τ¯bulk−τwt)LFC].\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Delta s_{i,{\text{wt}}}\approx\Delta g_{i,{\text{wt}}}\left[(\bar{\lambda}^{{\text{bulk}}}-\lambda_{{\text{wt}}})+({\bar{\tau}}^{{\text{bulk}}}-\tau_{{\text{wt}}}){\text{LFC}}\right].$$\end{document}

Equation S107 depends on the mutant library abundance xlib\begin{document}$x_{{\text{lib}}}$\end{document} through the effective traits λ¯bulk\begin{document}$\bar {\lambda }^{{\mathrm{bulk}}}$\end{document} and τ¯bulk\begin{document}${\bar{\tau}}^{{\mathrm{bulk}}}$\end{document} of the bulk competition (Appendix 1—section S7). Inserting Equation S50; Equation S51 into Equation S107, we obtain(S108)Δsi,wt=Δgi,wtxlibglibxlibglib+(1−xlib)gwt⋅[Δλlib,wt+LFCΔτlib,wt],\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \begin{array}{ll} \Delta s_{i,\text{wt}} = \Delta g_{i,\text{wt}} & \dfrac{x_{\text{lib}} g_{\text{lib}}}{x_{\text{lib}} g_{\text{lib}} + (1 - x_{\text{lib}}) g_{\text{wt}}} \\ & \cdot \left[ \Delta \lambda_{\text{lib},\text{wt}} + \text{LFC} \Delta \tau_{\text{lib},\text{wt}} \right], \end{array}$$\end{document}

where Δλlib,wt=λlib−λwt\begin{document}$\Delta \lambda _{{\text{lib}},{\text{wt}}}= \lambda _{{\text{lib}}} - \lambda _{{\text{wt}}}$\end{document} is the difference in lag times, and Δτlib,wt=τlib−τwt\begin{document}$\Delta \tau _{{\text{lib}},{\text{wt}}}= \tau _{{\text{lib}}} - \tau _{{\text{wt}}}$\end{document} the difference in e-fold growth times (reciprocal growth rates), between the library (defined according to Equations S47 and S48) and the wild-type. All the dependence on the library relative abundance xlib\begin{document}$x_{{\mathrm{lib}}}$\end{document} is now contained in the fraction outside the square brackets in Equation S108.

Since the relative fitness of the mutant library as a whole compared to the wild-type in bulk competition is (using Equations S89a–S89d)(S109)slib,wtbulk=−τ¯bulkτlibτwtΔλlib,wt−τ¯bulkτlibτwtΔτlib,wtLFCbulk,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s_{\text{lib},\text{wt}}^{\text{bulk}} = -\,\dfrac{\bar{\tau}^{\text{bulk}}}{\tau_{\text{lib}}\tau_{\text{wt}}} \Delta \lambda_{\text{lib},\text{wt}} - \dfrac{\bar{\tau}^{\text{bulk}}}{\tau_{\text{lib}}\tau_{\text{wt}}} \Delta \tau_{\text{lib},\text{wt}} \text{LFC}^{\text{bulk}},$$\end{document}

we can rewrite Equation S108 as(S110)Δsi,wt=−xlibslib,wtbulkΔgi,wtgwt.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Delta s_{i,{\text{wt}}}= -x_{{\text{lib}}} s^{{\text{bulk}}}_{{\text{lib}},{\text{wt}}}\frac{\Delta g_{i,{\text{wt}}}}{g_{{\text{wt}}}}.$$\end{document}

This shows that a mutant library that is neutral relative to the wild-type in the bulk competition (slib,wtbulk=0\begin{document}$s^{{\text{bulk}}}_{{\text{lib}},{\text{wt}}}= 0$\end{document}) removes the error from higher-order interactions, even when that neutrality is based on a trade-off between growth rates and lag times (Δλlib,wt=−Δτlib,wtLFCbulk\begin{document}$\Delta \lambda _{{\text{lib}},{\text{wt}}}= - \Delta \tau _{{\text{lib}},{\text{wt}}}{\text{LFC}}^{{\text{bulk}}}$\end{document}). We note that the error of higher-order interactions (Equation S110) appears similar to the error from the frame of reference (Equation S88), but the former includes the relative mutant growth rate Δgi,wt/gwt\begin{document}$\Delta g_{i,{\mathrm{wt}}}/g_{{\mathrm{wt}}}$\end{document} as an additional pre-factor.

sec.title: Calculating the upper bound on relative abundance of the mutant library
sec.p: To calculate the maximum relative library abundance that keeps the relative error below the threshold ϵ\begin{document}$\(\epsilon \)$\end{document}, we input the absolute error in Equation S108 into the relative error bound of Equation S102 and rearrange to isolate the dependence on the library abundance xlib\begin{document}$x_{{\mathrm{lib}}}$\end{document}:(S111)xlibglibxlibglib+(1−xlib)gwt<ϵAi\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{x_{{\text{lib}}} g_{{\text{lib}}} }{x_{{\text{lib}}} g_{{\text{lib}}} + (1 - x_{{\text{lib}}})g_{{\text{wt}}}} \lt {\epsilon}A_{i}$$\end{document}

where(S112)Ai=|Si,wtpairΔgi,wt(Δλlib,wt+LFCΔτlib,wt)|\begin{document}$$\displaystyle A_i = \left| \frac{S^{\text{pair}}_{i,\text{wt}}} {\Delta g_{i,\text{wt}}\left(\Delta \lambda_{\text{lib,wt}} + \text{LFC}\Delta \tau_{\text{lib,wt}}\right)} \right| $$\end{document}

depends on the focal mutant i but does not depend on the library abundance xlib\begin{document}$x_{{\text{lib}}}$\end{document}. The left-hand side of Equation S111 varies between zero and one as a function of xlib\begin{document}$x_{{\mathrm{lib}}}$\end{document}. This means that if ϵAi>1\begin{document}$\epsilon A_{i} \gt 1$\end{document}, any value of xlib\begin{document}$x_{{\text{lib}}}$\end{document} will satisfy Equation S111, meaning that the relative error on mutant i\begin{document}$\(i\)$\end{document} from higher-order interactions will always be less than ϵ\begin{document}$\epsilon $\end{document}. For example, this holds when the mutant i\begin{document}$\(i\)$\end{document} has the same growth rate as the wild-type (Δgi,wt=0\begin{document}$\Delta g_{i,{\text{wt}}}= 0$\end{document}, which causes Ai→∞\begin{document}$A_{i} \to \infty $\end{document}), even if it varies in lag time and/or other mutants have variation in growth rates.

We thus next consider the case where ϵAi<1\begin{document}$\epsilon A_{i} \lt 1$\end{document}. We multiply both sides of Equation S111 by the denominator on the left-hand side (always positive) to obtain(S113)xlibglib<ϵAi(xlibglib+(1−xlib)gwt),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle x_{\text{lib}}g_{\text{lib}} \lt \epsilon A_i\left(x_{\text{lib}}g_{\text{lib}} + (1-x_{\text{lib}})g_{\text{wt}}\right), $$\end{document}

and then collect all the terms involving xlib\begin{document}$x_{{\mathrm{lib}}}$\end{document} on the left-hand side:(S114)xlib((1−ϵAi)glib+ϵAigwt)<ϵAigwt.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle x_{\text{lib}} ((1-{\epsilon}A_{i}) g_{\text{lib}}+ {\epsilon}A_{i} g_{\text{wt}}) \lt {\epsilon}A_{i} g_{\text{wt}}.$$\end{document}

Since ϵAi<1\begin{document}${\epsilon}A_{i} \lt 1$\end{document}, the factor multiplying xlib\begin{document}$x_{{\mathrm{lib}}}$\end{document} on the left-hand side of Equation S114 must be positive and thus we can divide both sides to obtain an upper bound on the library abundance xlib\begin{document}$x_{{\mathrm{lib}}}$\end{document} such that the relative error on fitness is less than ϵ\begin{document}${\epsilon}$\end{document}:(S115)xlib<ϵAigwt(1−ϵAi)glib+ϵAigwt.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle x_{{\text{lib}}} \lt \frac{ {\epsilon}A_{i} g_{{\text{wt}}}}{(1-{\epsilon}A_{i}) g_{{\text{lib}}}+ {\epsilon}A_{i} g_{{\text{wt}}}}.$$\end{document}

Since ϵ\begin{document}$\({\epsilon}\)$\end{document} will typically be small, we can simplify the right-hand side of Equation S115 by approximating it to first-order in ϵ\begin{document}$\({\epsilon}\)$\end{document}:(S116)xlib⪅ϵAigwtglib.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle x_{{\text{lib}}} \lessapprox {\epsilon}A_{i} \frac{g_{{\text{wt}}}}{g_{{\text{lib}}}}.$$\end{document}
This approximation holds as long as ϵAi(glib−gwt)/glib≪1\begin{document}${\epsilon}A_{i}(g_{{\mathrm{lib}}} - g_{{\mathrm{wt}}})/g_{{\mathrm{lib}}} \ll 1$\end{document}.

The maximum mutant library abundance determined by Equation S115 or Equation S116 is specific to a single mutant genotype i, meaning that the relative fitness errors for other mutants may exceed ϵ\begin{document}$\({\epsilon}\)$\end{document} even if the inequality for mutant i is satisfied. To keep the relative fitness errors for all mutants less than ϵ\begin{document}${\epsilon}$\end{document}, we need to choose a library abundance xlib∗\begin{document}$x^{*}_{{\mathrm{lib}}}$\end{document} such that(S117)maxmut j|Δsj,wtsj,wtpair|<ϵ.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \max_{\mathrm{mut}~j} \left| \frac{\Delta s_{j,\mathrm{wt}}}{s^{\mathrm{pair}}_{j,\mathrm{wt}}} \right| \lt \epsilon. $$\end{document}

This means that Equation S116 must be satisfied for all mutants j:(S118)xlib∗=minmutsjϵAjgwtglib.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle x^{*}_{\mathrm{lib}} = \min _{{\mathrm{muts}\,j}}{\epsilon}A_{j} \frac{g_{\mathrm{wt}}}{g_{\mathrm{lib}}}.$$\end{document}

Thus, we must determine the minimum value of Aj\begin{document}$A_{j}$\end{document} over all mutants j. Using the definition in Equation S112, Aj\begin{document}$A_{j}$\end{document} is minimized for the mutant with minimum value of(S119)|sj,wtpairΔgj,wt|=|1gwtLFC−gjΔλj,wtΔgj,wt|,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left|\frac{s^{\mathrm{pair}}_{j,\mathrm{wt}}}{\Delta g_{j,\mathrm{wt}}}\right| = \left| \frac{1}{g_{\mathrm{wt}}}\mathrm{LFC} - g_j\frac{\Delta \lambda_{j,\mathrm{wt}}}{\Delta g_{j,\mathrm{wt}}} \right| ,$$\end{document}

where we have calculated the pairwise relative fitness in Equation S103 using tsatpair,i\begin{document}${t^{{\mathrm{pair}},i}_{\mathrm{sat}}}$\end{document} from Equation S106. Mutants that minimize Equation S119 are those with trade-offs between lag times and growth rates such that their overall pairwise relative fitness with respect to the wild-type is zero. This makes sense, since these mutants will have a relative fitness close to zero in the pairwise competition (|sj,wtpair|≪1\begin{document}$|s^{{\mathrm{pair}}}_{j,{\mathrm{wt}}}| \ll 1$\end{document}), but nonzero fitness relative to the wild-type in the bulk competition as the relative selection on the lag time and growth rate shifts (e.g., because τ¯bulk>τ¯pair\begin{document}${\bar{\tau}}^{{\mathrm{bulk}}} \gt {\bar{\tau}}^{{\mathrm{pair}}}$\end{document} in Equations S89a–S89d).

sec.title: Special case of variation in growth rates only
sec.p: To determine an even simpler estimate on the maximum mutant library abundance, we consider the special case where genotypes vary only in growth rates and not lag times. Using the definition in Equation S112, Ai=glib/(gwt−glib)\begin{document}$A_{i} = g_{{\mathrm{lib}}}/(g_{{\mathrm{wt}}} - g_{{\mathrm{lib}}})$\end{document} for all mutants i, and thus there is a single bound on library abundance for all mutants (using Equation S116):(S120)xlib<ϵ|gwtgwt−glib|.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle x_{\text{lib}} \lt \epsilon \left| \frac{g_{\text{wt}}}{g_{\text{wt}} - g_{\text{lib}}} \right| .$$\end{document}
This is the same as Equation 11 in the main text.

We test Equation 11 using our simulated competition data for the yeast single-gene deletion library (Methods) with variation in all three traits: lag time, growth rate, and biomass yield (Appendix 1—figure 4B, C). We compute the growth rates of the mutant library (glib=0.389hr−1\begin{document}$g_{{\mathrm{lib}}} = 0.389\,\mathrm{hr}^{-1}$\end{document} using Equation S40) and the wild-type (gwt=0.406hr−1\begin{document}$g_{{\mathrm{wt}}} =0.406\,\mathrm{hr}^{-1}$\end{document}). Using a relative error threshold of ϵ=0.01\begin{document}${\epsilon}= 0.01$\end{document}, the maximum mutant library relative abundance according to main text Equation 11 is xlib=24.6%\begin{document}$x_{{\mathrm{lib}}} = 24.6\%$\end{document}. Figure 5D in the main text shows that this mutant library abundance indeed is able to keep the relative error below the threshold for mutants with high relative fitness, but, as expected, this mutant library abundance fails for mutants close to neutrality.

We furthermore compute the maximum library abundance with Equation S118, based on the precise trait variation in our data set. The mutant library has an effective lag time λlib=1.95hr\begin{document}$\lambda _{{\mathrm{lib}}} = 1.95\, \mathrm{hr}$\end{document} (compared to wild-type lag time λwt=1.92hr\begin{document}$\lambda _{{\mathrm{wt}}}=1.92\,\mathrm{hr}$\end{document}) and an effective e\begin{document}$\(e\)$\end{document}-fold growth time τlib=2.57hr\begin{document}$\tau _{{\mathrm{lib}}} = 2.57\, \mathrm{hr}$\end{document} (compared to the wild-type τwt=2.46hr\begin{document}$\tau _{{\mathrm{wt}}} = 2.46\,\mathrm{hr}$\end{document}), leading to an overall negative relative fitness slib,wtbulk=−0.198\begin{document}$s^{{\mathrm{bulk}}}_{{\mathrm{lib}},{\mathrm{wt}}}= -0.198$\end{document} based on an LFC value of LFCbulk=log⁡100\begin{document}${\mathrm{LFC}}^{{\mathrm{bulk}}} = \log 100$\end{document} (a typical fold-change in our data set) and the limit of low relative abundance of the library. We insert these trait values into Equation S118 and obtain a maximum mutant library abundance xlib∗=0.01%\begin{document}$x_{{\mathrm{lib}}}^{*} = 0.01\%$\end{document}. Figure 5D in the main text shows that this much smaller mutant library abundance is able to keep the relative error below the desired threshold for all mutant genotypes. Note, however, this is still not fully exact since we have ignored the underlying variation in biomass yield in our trait data set.

body.p: This manuscript applies a theoretical analysis to two published datasets on yeast and bacterial evolution to compare different ways of quantifying fitness. It makes an important advance by clarifying how discrepancies can arise by using different approaches and provides recommendations for best practices. Overall, this is an impressive and highly beneficial study that is based on convincing evidence and has the potential of setting standards in this rapidly growing field.

[Editors' note: this version has been assessed by the Reviewing Editor without further input from the original reviewers. The authors have addressed the comments raised in the previous round of review.]

The authors point out that the fitness estimates obtained from different experimental assays (monoculture, pairwise competition or bulk competition) are not generally equivalent, not even with regard to the fitness ranking of different genotypes. Using a computational model based on experimentally measured growth phenotypes for knockout strains in yeast, as well as data from Lenski's Long Term Evolution Experiment (LTEE), they derive a set of best practice rules aimed at extracting the optimal amount of information from such experiments.
The study is very complete on a technical level, and the conceptual weaknesses raised in the first round of reviews have been fully addressed in the revision.

The manuscript "Quantifying microbial fitness in high-throughput experiments" provides a comprehensive analysis of the various approaches to quantifying fitness in microbial evolution, focusing on three primary factors: encoding of relative abundance, time scale of measurement, and the choice of reference subpopulation. The authors systematically explore how these choices impact fitness statistics and provide recommendations aimed at standardizing practices in the field. This manuscript aims to highlight the impact of differing fitness definitions and the methodologies utilized for analysis and how that can significantly alter interpretations of mutant fitness, affecting evolutionary predictions and the overall understanding of genetic interactions in the experiments.

The choices for quantifying fitness in evolution experiments are critical and highly relevant given the increasing prevalence of high-throughput experiments in evolutionary biology. The authors methodically categorize fitness statistics and their implications, providing clarity on a complex subject. This structured approach aids in understanding the nuances of fitness measurement. The manuscript effectively highlights how different choices in fitness measurement can influence fitness rankings and the understanding of epistasis, which is important for modeling evolutionary dynamics.

The authors have comprehensively addressed all previous comments and suggestions. In particular, the addition of the new methods section: 'A guide to calculate pairwise relative fitness under the logit encoding from bulk competition data' - significantly improves the clarity of the implementation and helps in the overall interpretation of the framework.

The authors present analyses of different fitness measures derived from empirical data from yeast knock-out mutants and the long-term evolution experiment (LTEE) with Escherichia coli to explore discrepancies and identify preferred methods to estimate relative fitness in high-throughput experiments. Their work has three components. They first discuss the different "encodings" of relative abundance data and conclude that logit-transformations are preferred, because they transform nonlinear abundance trajectories into linear trajectories with greater predictive power. Next, they compare per-generation with per-growth cycle relative fitness estimates inferred from simulations of pairwise competitions based on published growth traits for the yeast strains and on published pairwise competition measurements for the LTEE data. Both data sets show quantitative and qualitative (i.e. rank order) discrepancies of estimates across different time scales, which are highlighted by considering possible underlying causes (i.e. trade-offs between growth traits) and consequences (i.e. epistasis among mutations affecting different growth traits). Finally, the authors compare simulated pairwise and bulk (i.e. where many mutants compete during a growth cycle in a single environment) competition assays based on the yeast knock-out mutants and demonstrate an optimal ratio of collective mutants to wild-type strains that minimizes both sampling error and overestimation of fitness estimates when compared with pairwise competitions.

The study deals with a highly relevant topic. Fitness is central to general evolutionary theory, but also poorly defined and implies different traits for different organisms and conditions. For microbes, which are often used in evolution experiments, high-throughput experiments may yield different measures to quantify abundance over time, from individual growth traits to bulk competition experiments. Hence, it is relevant to consider discrepancies among those measures and identify preferred measures with respect to predicting population dynamic and evolutionary processes. The present study contributes to this aim by (i) making readers aware of differences among commonly used fitness estimates, (ii) showing that simulated (yeast) and calculated (E. coli) competitive fitness may differ across time scales, and (iii) showing that bulk competitions may yield relative fitness estimates that are systematically higher than pairwise competitions. The study is rather thorough on the theory side, with extensive derivations and analyses of various fitness measures using their resource competition model in the Supplementary Information. The study ends with a few practical recommendations for preferred methods to infer relative fitness estimates, that may be useful for experimentalists and stimulate further investigations.
I appreciate the thorough and effective response to all recommendations and have no further comments.
